title: Little Men

subtitle.text: Hello! My name is Jo Bauer, but readers of [i@Little Women@i] may remember me as Jo March.
Yes, I married Professor Fritz Bauer, and we operate a school called Plumfield.
It's a few miles outside the town where I lived with my sisters, Meg, Beth, and Amy.
Poor Beth passed away, but my other sisters are married and leading happy lives.
My younger sister, Amy, is an artist and married to Theodore Laurence.
We call him Laurie because we've known him for years.
When we were growing up, he lived next door to us, and his tutor, John Brookes, married my older sister.
Meg and John have ten-year-old twins.
Demi is a Plumfield student, and Daisy is staying with us because Meg recently had another baby.
But that's enough about the past. It's time to meet the Little Men of Plumfield—and Daisy too!
One rainy spring Saturday, a ragged 12-year-old boy arrived at the door of a large, comfortable house.
He gave a timid rap with the brass knocker.
Although he could hear children playing inside, no one came to the door.
He knocked again, but when no one answered, he hesitantly pushed open the door.
And what a sight greeted him!
Two boys about his age were playing tag while two younger boys chased a yellow puppy and a white one.
Another boy sat quietly reading on the stairs.
"Oh, hello!" A dark-haired girl looked up from her doll. "Are you a new boy?"
"I don't know yet," he said shyly.
"My name's Nat Blake, and I have a letter for Mrs. Bauer from Mr. Theodore Laurence.
He said she'd take care of me."
"Wait here, and I'll take Uncle Laurie's letter to Aunt Jo.
I'm Daisy, and that's my brother, Demi."
Daisy pointed to the boy reading on the stairs, oblivious to what was happening around him.
Suddenly one of the tag players slid down the banister.
Unable to stop, the boy landed with a crash that would have knocked anyone else unconscious.
Nat forgot his shyness and ran over, expecting to find the boy half-dead.
However, the boy simply blinked rapidly and looked up at Nat.
"Have you come to join us? I'm Tommy Bangs."
Tommy jumped up, as if he'd just remembered his manners.
"Come play tag with Jack Ford and me!"
"I should probably wait to see whether I'm staying," Nat mumbled, looking around.
He saw a large schoolroom and a cozy parlor.
A dining room had a table set for supper.
As the smell of gingerbread filled the air, Nat's desire to stay grew.
Daisy returned with the news that Nat was to stay.
She led him to Jo's study.
"I'm delighted to see you!"
Jo smoothed the hair from Nat's forehead.
"I hope you'll be happy here. Oh my, but your feet are wet!"
Jo bustled around and found Nat some slippers.
She smiled at him.
"These are too big, but that'll keep you from running away."
"I don't want to run away, ma'am—" Nat dissolved in a fit of coughing.
"How long have you been sick?" Jo asked, looking concerned.
"I caught a cold this winter and never recovered," Nat said when he could speak again.
"Sit by the fire, and we'll get some medicine into you."
Nat had just swallowed a spoonful of medicine when the bell rang for supper.
Jo led him into the dining room, where he found a cheerful man sitting with six children.
"Nat, this is my husband, Professor Bauer," Jo said.
"And I think you've already met our two sons, Rob and Teddy.
This is Jack, Tommy, Demi, and Daisy."
Nat nodded shyly and took the empty seat next to Tommy.
"Where did you used to go to school?" Tommy asked.
"I didn't," Nat said, and Tommy's eyes widened in surprise.
"I worked on the city streets, playing the fiddle with my father and a man named Nicolo."
"That sounds like fun!" Tommy said.
"It wasn't—I never had enough to eat."
Nat paused to take a bite of gingerbread.
"After my father died and I got sick, Nicolo took away my fiddle."
"I bet Mr. Bauer will let you play his old fiddle," Tommy said, making Nat's face brighten with pleasure.
Sure enough, after supper Jo handed a violin to Nat, and he began playing softly.
As his confidence grew, the other children stepped closer.
"Hey, you're good!" Tommy said.
"Play something we know, and we'll sing along."
Soon everyone was singing, but as the last notes died away, Nat began to sob.
"Nat, what is it?" Jo asked with alarm.
"You're all so kind, and—" Nat coughed until he was breathless.
Jo wrapped her arms around him.
"You have a father and mother now, and this is your home.
Don't think of those sad times anymore."
Nat gulped and managed a smile.
After a bath, Nat relaxed in front of the fire while Jo bathed Teddy and Rob.
When a pillow fight broke out, Jo laughed.
"Aren't you going to punish those boys?" Nat asked.
"Of course not," Jo said as Tommy ran into the room and tossed a pillow at her.
She fired it right back at him.
"Our boys do whatever they want on Saturdays, and that includes pillow fights."
"What a nice school this is!" Nat sighed.
"It's an odd one," Jo admitted, "but we don't believe in making children miserable with too many rules and too much studying."
On Sunday morning Nat eagerly ran downstairs, but he started coughing as soon as he greeted Jo.
"No church for you today," Jo said with a frown.
"You should stay home with my sons and me."
"But they're practically babies, and I'm 12 years—" Nat's coughs interrupted his protest.
So Nat spent the morning in Jo's study, learning a hymn and listening to her read aloud.
Jo showed him her "Sunday closet," which was filled with books, art supplies, and building blocks.
"I want everyone to treat Sunday as a day for quiet activities," she explained.
"But you can still learn things on Sundays."
"You mean lessons about how to be good?"
Jo nodded and reached for a thick book, filled with handwritten pages.
She flipped to a page with only one word at the top: Nat.
"That's my name!" he cried, looking both surprised and interested.
"Yes, I have a page for each boy.
I keep track of how he behaves during the week and show it to him on Sunday night.
If the report is bad, I'm disappointed; if it's good, I'm proud," Jo went on.
"No matter what, I hope the boys know I want to help them.
I also hope they'll try their best because they love Mr. Bauer and me."
"Oh, I'll try to make you proud!"
Jo hugged Nat. "I'll be happy if you follow our few rules, get along with the other boys, and learn something."
After lunch Jo took her sons and Daisy into town to visit family.
Everyone else went for a long walk, but Nat wasn't strong enough for that much exercise.
So Tommy offered to show him the gardens and the animals.
First they strolled into the barn.
"We all have pets," Tommy explained, proudly showing off his guinea pig.
"Those white mice are Rob's, and Demi keeps turtles over there."
"What's in this box?" Nat asked, pointing to a deep box, half-full of dirt.
"That's Jack's worm farm.
He digs up worms and keeps them there until we go fishing so he can sell them to us.
Last time he charged me too much for some little worms.
But that's Jack—he loves money!"
"Who owns the puppies I saw in the house?" Nat asked.
"The white one is Rob's and the yellow one is Teddy's.
They like to chase Daisy's cat, Topaz."
Nat looked around the barn at all the animals.
"That donkey would be my first choice for a pet," he said, remembering how far he used to walk with his violin.
Riding a donkey would have saved him lots of time.
"Mr. Laurence gave Toby to Mrs. Bauer so she and Teddy can ride when we go for walks."
Nat shook his head in amazement. "Where do you get all these animals?"
"We find them or buy them, or people give them to us. My father sent mine.
Here, I'll show you my two chickens."
Nat sighed because he had neither the money to buy a pet nor a father to buy him one.
He followed Tommy into the hayloft.
"I'll tell you what I'll do," Tommy said.
"I hate hunting for eggs.
If you gather them, I'll give you one egg from every dozen.
I sell them to Mrs. Bauer, and when you've got a dozen, she'll pay you too."
"Then I can buy whatever I want!" Nat said, grinning at the prospect.
He quickly found two eggs, and Tommy generously let him keep one right away.
Then Tommy wrote "Tommy Bangs & Company" on the barn wall with a piece of chalk.
"You can keep track of your eggs here," Tommy said, handing Nat the chalk.
After that, the boys went outside, where Nat met two horses, six cows, one calf, and three pigs.
Tommy and Nat climbed into a willow tree that hung over a brook.
"You can see our gardens from here," Tommy said.
"Everybody grows a different type of plant."
"Do you think I'll have a garden?" Nat asked eagerly.
"Of course you will!" said a friendly voice below.
The boys looked down and saw the professor, who had just returned from his walk.
Nat easily climbed down from the tree, but Tommy fell into the brook!
"Are you okay?" Nat cried.
Tommy climbed out of the water with a rueful grin.
"Yeah, that happens all the time," he said and hurried to the house to dry off.
"How are things going?" the professor asked Nat.
"Are you prepared for school tomorrow?"
"Well . . ." Nat paused.
"I'm worried the boys will laugh when they see how little I know."
"Ah, but you have skills and qualities they lack.
You can play the violin, and you want to learn." Mr. Bauer patted Nat's shoulder.
"Don't worry—the boys will help you with your lessons."
And Nat soon found that to be true.
As time passed, he settled in, planting beans in his garden, and earning money by fiddling at neighbors' picnics.
"Oh, Fritz, he reminds me so much of Beth and her music," Jo whispered one evening as she and the professor listened to Nat.
"Yes, Nat's a good boy, although he sometimes tells lies.
Last week he denied stepping on plants in the garden, even though there were witnesses.
And today he lied to me about studying for a test."
"Nat learned from his father that lying is the best way to avoid punishment," Jo said.
"They're mostly small lies," the professor went on, "but nevertheless I'm afraid they'll get him into trouble one day."
"Aunt Jo," Daisy cried, dashing into Jo's study, "the boys won't let me play football!
They say girls can't play football."
"That's ridiculous!" Jo retorted, putting down her pen.
"I know girls can play because I did it when I was young."
Daisy sighed. "I'm tired of doing things by myself—will you play with me?"
"I will later, but right now I'm getting ready to go into town.
Come with me, and if you want, you can stay with your mother for a few days."
"I'd like to see Mama and baby Josy, but I don't want to stay with them.
Demi would miss me, and I love being here!"
"All right, but how will you entertain yourself until I'm ready?"
Daisy shrugged and said, "Can you make up a new game or activity for me?"
"Hmm, it'll take a while to think up something brand-new.
Why don't you see what Asia is preparing for lunch?"
"That's a good idea!" Daisy cried, running off to visit the cook in her kitchen.
In five minutes Daisy returned with a spot of flour on her nose.
"Please, Aunt Jo, may I make cookies with Asia?" she asked.
"I won't bother her, and it would be such fun!"
"Go ahead, and stay as long as you like," Jo said, relieved that Daisy had found something to do.
And suddenly Jo knew how to keep her niece entertained.
That afternoon Daisy visited her mother, Meg, while Jo went shopping.
Jo returned later with many mysterious parcels, but all she said was "They're for Daisy."
When it was time to leave, Meg tied Daisy's bonnet.
"Be a good girl for Aunt Jo.
She's very kind to think of this for you because she doesn't like this activity much herself."
At this, the two sisters burst out laughing, which only increased Daisy's curiosity.
All the way home, Daisy pestered Jo with questions.
"Have I ever seen this game before?"
"You've never seen one as nice as this," Jo replied.
Daisy heard something rattling in the back of the carriage.
"Is it for the boys too?" she asked.
"No, it's just for you and me and Bess," Jo said.
Bess was Daisy's cousin, Laurie and Amy's daughter.
"I ran into Uncle Laurie in town, and he helped me choose the different parts."
"Oh, the game must be wonderful because Uncle Laurie buys the best presents!" Daisy said.
By the time they reached home, Daisy was nearly wild with anticipation.
But Jo said Daisy couldn't do the new activity until she finished her lessons the next day.
Daisy's excitement soon spread to the boys, who offered to help Jo set up Daisy's present.
"Sorry, no boys allowed," Jo said, treating the four boys exactly as they'd treated Daisy.
At this, the boys meekly went away and sought out Daisy.
They offered to play football, marbles, or anything she liked, but Daisy only shook her head and smiled, delighted to turn them down.
The next morning Daisy quickly finished her lessons.
Jo took her up to the playroom, where Daisy heard something bubbling.
"It's a real little kitchen!" Daisy cried.
She ran over to the stove and saw a boiling tea kettle.
On either side of the stove were shelves filled with measuring cups, mixing bowls, and pots and pans.
Cabinets held spices and other ingredients.
"You had so much fun making cookies that I decided you needed a kitchen of your own," Jo explained.
"Why don't you pretend you're a cook now, and go to market."
Daisy looked perplexed. "But where's the market?" she asked.
"In Asia's kitchen, of course!"
Daisy went downstairs and returned with a potato, some squash, and the ingredients for a small pie.
With Jo's help, she quickly made the pie and put it in the oven.
Next she boiled the potato and steamed the squash.
After setting the table, she admired the contents of her kitchen as well as her new apron and cap.
But when she checked on her pie, she saw that disaster had struck!
"Aunt Jo! The pie burned!" Tears rolled down Daisy's face.
"Oh no!" Jo cried, putting down the book she was reading to Teddy.
"I should have paid more attention!" Using a potholder, she removed the blackened pastry from the oven.
"When we were shopping for your kitchen, Uncle Laurie took great delight in reminding me of my cooking disasters.
This pie isn't fit to eat, but I'm sure your dolls will enjoy the rest of the meal."
No sooner had Daisy settled her dolls at the table than the boys swarmed into the room.
"What are you cooking?" Demi asked.
"It smells delicious!" Nat added, rubbing his belly.
"Hey, that steamer looks like something we could use," Tommy said to Jack.
Daisy looked alarmed when Jack nodded in agreement and said, "That heavy pot would be perfect for melting down—"
"Aha!" Just then Mr. Bauer arrived.
"So this is your new kitchen, Daisy.
I hope you're a better cook than Aunt Jo!"
"All right, Fritz, that's enough!" Jo said, clapping her hands and frowning at her husband.
"Everyone out of the kitchen except Daisy!"
"But we haven't told Daisy what we want her to make for us!" Tommy protested.
"What about my favorite German dish—cabbage soup with herring and cherries?" Mr. Bauer suggested.
"I can't even make that!" Jo said, shaking her head.
But Daisy was ready for another cooking challenge.
"I'll give it a try, Uncle Fritz!" she said happily.
Nat stood at the door of Jo's study and peered inside.
"Please, ma'am, may I speak to you about something very important?"
Nat was the third boy who'd interrupted Jo in the last half hour, but she was used to distractions.
"What is it, my boy?" she asked.
Nat entered, shutting the door carefully behind him.
"Dan's here," he said eagerly.
"Who's Dan?" Jo asked.
"A boy I knew when I played the fiddle in the city.
He's 14, and he sold newspapers and was always kind to me.
Last week when Mr. Laurence took me to a concert in the city, I saw Dan on the street.
I told him how nice it was here, and now he's come to see for himself."
"This is a rather unexpected visit," Jo murmured, pushing back her chair.
"Oh, this isn't a visit—Dan has come to stay!" Nat said.
But when he caught the startled look on Jo's face, he corrected himself.
"I mean, if you'll allow him to stay."
"Well, I don't know about that yet," Jo began, caught off guard by the suddenness of this proposal.
"I thought you liked to take care of poor boys like me," Nat said.
"I do, but I can't take in every boy who comes to our door—there isn't room.
Besides, I like to choose who lives here."
"Dan could have my bed, and I could sleep in the barn," Nat said.
"I used to sleep anywhere with my father."
Jo was touched by Nat's confidence in her, and she didn't have the heart to spoil his plan.
"Bring him in, and we'll try to find space for him."
Nat happily ran off and soon returned, followed by a tall boy who gave Jo a hostile look from underneath his long black hair.
She instantly sensed he was a troublemaker.
"This is Dan," Nat said.
"Nat tells me you'd like to stay with us," Jo began in a friendly tone.
"It sounds like you don't have anywhere else to go?"
"Nope."
"Say, 'No, ma'am,'" Nat whispered.
"I won't!" Dan muttered.
Jo ignored this conversation and went on.
"If you stay here, we'll expect you to work and study as well as play.
Are you willing to agree to that?"
"Don't mind trying."
"You can stay a few days, and we'll see how we get along."
Jo had never met a boy with such a hard, suspicious face.
"Please take him outside, Nat, and introduce him to the other boys."
"Thank you, ma'am!" Nat said.
Outside, Nat led Dan to the barn.
"We're having a circus!" he said.
Nat and Dan joined Rob and Jack in the audience.
Bales of hay marked a wide circle on the barn floor.
Demi stood in the middle with a whip, while Tommy rode Toby the donkey, pretending he was a horse.
The next act featured Jack dancing a fine jig, and then Tommy proudly turned a somersault, a trick he'd been working on for weeks.
"That's not really a trick!" Dan said, laughing.
"Hey!" Tommy scowled as he rubbed his sore elbows. "Don't insult me!"
"I'll insult whoever I want," Dan said, approaching Tommy and holding up his fists like he meant business.
"Do you want to fight?"
"Uh, not really," Tommy muttered and took a step back.
"Fighting isn't allowed!" the others cried.
"Well, aren't you a nice little group," Dan said with a sneer.
"If you don't behave, Dan, you won't be allowed to stay," Nat said, annoyed that Dan was insulting his friends.
"I'd just like to see him perform better than I did," Tommy said.
"Get out of the way then!" Dan replied, barely pausing before he turned three somersaults, one after the other, and landed on his feet.
"You can't beat that, Tommy," Nat said.
Before Nat could say another word, Dan did three backward somersaults followed by a short walk on his hands.
This impressed everyone, and even Tommy joined in the cries of admiration.
Dan looked at his audience with an air of calm superiority.
"Do you think I could learn to do that without getting hurt?" Tommy asked Dan.
"What will you give me if I teach you?"
"My new pocket knife has five blades, and only one is broken."
"Hand it over."
Tommy reluctantly gave his knife to Dan, who examined it and started to walk away.
"Here's my advice: keep practicing until you learn how to do it."
A howl of wrath from Tommy was followed by everyone running after Dan.
"Give him back his knife right now!" Nat said.
After Dan obeyed, Nat grabbed Dan's arm.
"And now you're going for a walk with me!"
No one knew what Nat said to Dan, but when they reappeared, Dan was more respectful toward everyone.
The boys still didn't like Dan and left him to Nat, who soon felt burdened by his old friend.
When Mr. Bauer heard the story of Dan's first day, he shook his head.
"We may have made a mistake by taking him in," he said to Jo.
"But only time will tell."
As time passed, Jo lost her patience with Dan half a dozen times a day, but she didn't give up on him.
"I know there's some good inside Dan," she said to her husband.
"He may be rude to people, but he's kind to animals, and Teddy is so fond of him."
It was true. Dan was very affectionate with little Teddy, who called him my Danny.
To Jo, these were signs that she could eventually win Dan over.
As the days passed, Tommy and Jack began to admire Dan because he was courageous.
Demi, who loved to read, regarded Dan as a walking storybook.
That was because Dan could describe his adventures in a most exciting way.
It pleased Dan that the boys liked him, so he made an effort to be friendly.
But he felt that Jo and the professor didn't trust him, so he took delight in trying their patience.
One of Mr. Bauer's strictest rules was no fighting.
"You should never fight," he reminded the boys one day.
"It's not an effective way to settle a dispute or entertain others."
"What a stupid rule!" Dan said under his breath.
Later that afternoon the boys were bored and looking for something interesting to do.
"Tell us another story about a fight you won," Demi said.
"Never mind that," Tommy said, "I'd like to learn how to box!"
"I'll teach you, but do you promise not to tell Mr. Bauer?" Dan asked.
"Oh, yes!" they all cried at once.
The boys went behind the barn, where Dan proceeded to give them boxing lessons.
That was enough to satisfy Demi, Tommy, and Nat, but Jack wanted a real fight.
"Come on!" Jack challenged Dan. "I bet I could beat you!"
"Yeah," Tommy shouted, "let's see a fight!"
Dan pulled off his jacket, and the match began.
But just as the boys started punching each other, Mr. Bauer rushed toward them.
"Stop this at once!" he roared, separating the two fighters.
"You should be ashamed of yourselves!"
"Let me go!" Dan shouted.
His shirt was torn, and his eye was beginning to swell shut.
Jack's chin was covered with blood from a cut lip.
"You know fighting's forbidden here, right?" Mr. Bauer asked Dan in his angriest voice.
"Yes," Dan growled.
"Then why did you break the rule?"
"Every fellow needs to learn to defend himself."
"These boys will do fine without learning how to injure each other.
Now go wash up, Jack and Dan, and remember, Dan, if you break any more rules, you'll be sent away."
But that warning only served as a challenge to Dan, who was soon in trouble again.
A week later the boys were out making fishing poles from sticks.
On the way home, Tommy was riding the donkey, Toby, and carrying his new pole.
"You look just like a bullfighter, Tommy," Demi said, thinking of a picture in one of his favorite books.
"Only you're not wearing fancy clothes or carrying a red cloth."
"Let's have a bullfight!" Dan said, intent on making mischief.
"Ride at that old cow over there in the meadow—let's see her run."
"Don't annoy Buttercup!" Demi said.
"You're always such a good little boy," Dan said in a nasty tone.
"Why shouldn't we do it?"
"I don't think my uncle Fritz would like it."
"Did he ever forbid bullfights?" Dan demanded.
"No, I don't think so," Demi admitted.
"Then be quiet," Dan said as he pulled a red handkerchief from his pocket.
"Here's a rag to wave at the cow, Tommy. I'll help you stir her up."
Dan went over the pasture wall with the others following right behind.
Even Demi sat atop the wall and watched the scene with great interest.
Tommy rode toward Buttercup and tapped her with his fishing pole.
"Moo!" cried the surprised animal.
"That's it!" Dan called. "Come on, Nat and Jack! Tap her with your poles."
Poor Buttercup trotted around the field, getting more confused and excited every moment.
No matter which way she turned, there was a boy with a pole.
All at once she leaped over the wall and ran out of sight down the road.
"Catch her!" Dan shouted.
"If anything happens to her, Mr. Bauer will send me away!"
Buttercup may have been old, but she led the boys on a merry chase.
At last they caught her in a neighbor's flower garden.
Borrowing a rope, Dan led her home, followed by a group of solemn boys and the donkey.
"Look, Dan, she's all wet and muddy, and she's limping!" Nat said.
"You're in trouble now," Tommy added.
"So are you," Dan said.
"We all helped except for Demi," Jack said, "but he was the one who first mentioned bullfighting."
"I told Dan not to do it!" Demi protested.
"Well, I guess this is the end for me," Dan said, "but I don't care."
When the professor saw Buttercup and heard the story, he said little.
He sent the boys to their rooms, which gave them time to worry about their punishment.
The longer Dan sat on his bed, the more he thought about the warmth and kindness he'd received here,
and the hardship and neglect he'd felt elsewhere.
But he knew the Bauers were finished with him.
"I've lived on the streets before," he told himself defiantly, "and I can do it again!"
So he was ready when Mr. Bauer finally knocked on his door.
"You've greatly disappointed us, especially because you're usually so kind to animals," the professor began.
He went on, and the more he talked, the worse Dan felt.
"Why doesn't he hurry up and throw me out?" Dan thought as he stared at the floor.
"However," the professor concluded, "I'm giving you one more chance because Mrs. Bauer believes in you. Shall we try again?"
Dan looked up in surprise at this unexpected kindness and blurted out, "Yes, please!"
After the incident with Buttercup, Dan tried to behave for a few days.
But it wasn't long before he went back to his old ways.
"Let's have some fun," he said one night to Nat.
He pulled a bottle of root beer, a small cake, and some cards from under his bed.
Nat's eyes widened. "Where did you get that food?" he asked.
"It was sitting in the kitchen all day," Dan explained with a shrug.
"Asia always tells me I can help myself to snacks.
Besides, nobody is around—Mr. Bauer's away, and Mrs. Bauer is busy with Teddy, who's sick or something.
Don't you want to learn how to play poker?"
Tempted by the adventure, Nat nodded.
"Well, we need another player, so go get Tommy, and bring a candle for more light."
"I'll bring Demi too," said Nat, who shared a room with Demi.
"No, he'll just tell on us or try to stop us. Besides, he's probably asleep."
Nat ran off and returned with a candle and Tommy, who was always ready for fun.
"First we'll eat, and then we'll play cards for money," Dan said as he passed the root beer and cake around.
"That's what real men do."
"I wish we didn't have to be so quiet," Tommy said softly.
"But we don't want Silas to hear us."
Silas managed the property for Mr. Bauer, and his room was right next door.
Suddenly a voice in the hall wailed, "I can't find Nat!"
Then the boys heard the patter of bare feet.
"It's Demi, and he's gone to get Mrs. Bauer," Dan cried, whisking everything out of sight.
"Get in bed, everyone!"
Tommy and Nat flew to their rooms.
Hearing Demi's voice again, Nat quickly blew out his candle and tossed it under his bed.
When Demi arrived with Jo a few seconds later, Nat was pretending to be asleep.
But Jo wasn't fooled. "What mischief are you up to?"
"What?" Nat said sleepily.
"I only ran into Dan's room for a minute . . . I'm so sleepy . . . "
Jo gave up and returned to Teddy, and Nat was soon asleep for real.
Little did he realize what was happening under his bed—the candle was not out!
Meanwhile Silas had awakened because he smelled something burning.
Poking his head into the hall, he saw smoke coming from Nat and Demi's room.
"Fire! Fire!" Silas cried, running to rescue the sleeping boys.
Nat's bed was on fire, and the flames were licking the curtains.
By the time Silas had pulled Nat and Demi to safety, Jo was on the scene.
"Dan! Jack! Bring water from the bathroom!
Tommy, get more buckets from the kitchen!
Daisy, tell Asia I need her right now!
Rob, stay out of the way!"
The fire was quickly under control.
Demi was more frightened than hurt, but Nat had a painful burn on his arm.
When Mr. Bauer returned the next day, the boys gathered around him.
Nat and Tommy immediately apologized for lying about the poker game, and the danger they'd caused, but Dan remained defiant.
"You know I hate gambling, Dan," the professor said with a frown.
"And you took a treat that Asia had left for Silas!
Worst of all, you've involved the other boys in your misdeeds."
"I didn't know it was a treat for Silas," Dan snapped.
"Besides, not much harm was done."
"Not much harm?" The professor raised his eyebrows in surprise.
"The burn on Nat's arm is a terrible punishment, and Tommy is truly sorry. But you, Dan, have not even apologized.
We've forgiven you many times, but it has done no good—you're still setting a bad example.
So say good-bye to everyone, and pack up your things."
"Where's he going?" Nat cried.
"To Mr. Page's school in the country because Mr. Page has straightened out many troubled boys."
"Will he ever come back?" Demi asked.
"I hope so, but that's up to Dan himself," Mr. Bauer said.
After Mr. Bauer left the room, the boys were full of questions for Dan.
"Will you like it at Mr. Page's school?" Jack asked.
"I won't stay if I don't," Dan replied.
"Where would you go?" Nat asked.
"Maybe I'll go to sea or out to California," Dan said with a reckless air that startled the boys.
"Oh, don't do that! Stay with Mr. Page awhile and then come back here," Nat pleaded.
"I'm never coming back [i@here@i]!" Dan stormed upstairs to pack his things, every one of which Mr. Bauer had given him.
When it was time to leave, Jo came outside, looking so sad that Dan felt remorseful.
"May I go in to say good-bye to Teddy?" he asked.
"Yes, he'll miss his Danny very much," Jo said, and followed him upstairs.
While Dan was bending over Teddy's bed, he heard Jo talking to her husband.
"Can't we give him another chance—he's the only boy we've ever failed with."
But Mr. Bauer's mind was firmly made up.
Dan wanted to ask for one more chance, but his pride wouldn't allow him.
So, with a stony look on his face, he climbed into the wagon.
A few days later, Mr. Page sent a letter, saying Dan was doing well.
But three weeks later, another letter arrived, and this one said that Dan had run away.
Mr. Bauer sighed. "Perhaps I should have given him another chance."
"Don't worry, Fritz," Jo said. "I'm sure he'll come back to us."
But time passed, and Dan did not return.
"Fritz, let's enroll another girl in the school," Jo said one morning.
"Daisy needs a playmate, and another girl would improve the boys' behavior."
Mr. Bauer nodded. "Do you have anyone in mind?" he asked.
"Annie Harding," Jo said.
Annie was a ten-year-old who'd lost her mother.
Jo had run into her father in town recently.
"Naughty Nan!" Mr. Bauer exclaimed.
"That's what the boys call her," Jo said, "but I just see a girl running wild since her mother died.
I was such a naughty child myself, and I remember how much my mother helped me.
I've already talked to Nan's father—since he and Nan are visiting some friends nearby today,
he's going to drop her off this afternoon, if that's all right."
"As far as I'm concerned, you can bring home a dozen Nans," said Mr. Bauer, who loved children.
"I doubt she'll turn out to be another troublemaker."
Jo sighed. "I can never forgive myself for letting Dan go."
When Nan arrived, she ran into the house, shouting for Daisy.
Daisy came downstairs, pleased to see the other girl.
"My big suitcase is coming tomorrow by train because we couldn't fit it in our carriage today," Nan announced.
"I'm going to stay here forever!"
"Oh my!" Daisy looked somewhat alarmed at that news, but she quickly recovered and remembered to be polite.
"Do you want to play in my kitchen?"
"No, I want to see the boys and the barn."
Nan took off, swinging her hat by one string until it broke.
She left her hat where it fell on the grass.
Daisy followed Nan to the barn and found the boys sitting outside.
"I'm here and I'm going to stay!" Nan said.
"Hooray!" Tommy liked Nan because she was always ready for adventure.
"Let's play baseball," Nan said.
"We just finished a game," Demi said, resting against the barn wall.
"How about a race—I bet I can beat you all," Nan said.
Nat looked at Tommy and asked if it was true.
"I hate to admit it, but she's really fast," Tommy said.
"She's still a girl," Jack said, "and all girls are crybabies."
"I never cry no matter how badly I'm hurt!" Nan said, sounding insulted.
"I could make you cry in two seconds."
Jack pointed to some plants at the edge of the field.
"Go pick some of those stinging nettles over there."
Nan instantly grabbed a bunch of plants with both hands and held on, despite the pain.
After that, even Jack had to admit Nan wasn't a crybaby.
That night at supper, Mr. Bauer officially welcomed Nan to Plumfield.
He held out his hand for her to shake, but Nan kept her hands behind her back.
"What's wrong with your hands?" the professor asked.
Daisy took a deep breath and told the adults the whole story.
"Oh, your poor hands!" Mr. Bauer looked at Jo, and both of them smiled slightly.
Nan had been there only a few hours, and already she was stirring things up.
"Do you know why I asked Nan to come stay with us?" Jo said to the boys.
"To help me make gentlemen of you."
"I hate boys!" Nan said fiercely.
"I'm sorry to hear that—our boys can be quite nice when they try," Jo said.
The boys took the hint, and for the rest of supper, they were very polite to Nan.
The first thing Nan said the next morning was "Has my suitcase arrived?"
"It's supposed to come sometime today," Jo said.
Nan was disappointed but somehow managed to survive.
Only at suppertime did Jo realize she was missing.
"I saw her running down the drive earlier," Asia said.
"I hope she hasn't gone home," Jo said.
"Maybe she went to the train station to fetch her suitcase," Demi suggested.
"She doesn't know the way," Mr. Bauer said, "and besides, how could she carry such a heavy load back here?"
"Nan could probably figure out all that," Jo said.
She couldn't help smiling even as she worried about Nan.
"But why don't you take the carriage, Fritz, and search for her."
"There she is!" shouted Rob, who was looking out the window.
Nan was struggling up the drive with her suitcase.
When the boys rushed out to help her, she insisted on carrying her load as far as the steps.
Then she plopped on top of the suitcase.
"I couldn't wait any longer for it to be delivered," she said.
"But the station's a mile away!" Tommy said.
"How did you even find it?"
"I can always find my way," Nan said proudly.
"I'm surprised the stationmaster let you take it," Demi said.
"He was in the ticket office, so I just took it off the platform," Nan said.
Jo shook her head at this new problem.
"Go tell the stationmaster what's happened, Fritz.
Otherwise he'll think Nan's suitcase was stolen."
By now all the boys thought Nan was brave, and at supper she entertained them with her adventures.
"You're going to have your hands full with that girl," Mr. Bauer later said to Jo.
Unfortunately for Jo, his prediction came true.
Nan got into mischief, partly because she did whatever the boys dared her to do.
But there was another side to Nan:
she was generous with her toys and thought up new games for Daisy and Rob.
And when the professor challenged her to do better than the boys at school, Nan beat them in the classroom too.
Mrs. Shakespeare Smith had sent the boys an invitation to a special ball.
"It says here, Nat, that you should bring your violin so everyone can dance," Tommy said.
"And it indicates that we must behave if we want anything to eat."
"I've never been to a ball," Nat said, "and who is Mrs. Shakespeare Smith?"
Demi grinned. "That's a name Daisy uses sometimes.
She pretends she's a grown-up, and Nan is her daughter, Miss Smith."
"The ball's today at three o'clock in the playroom," Jack said, looking at the invitation.
"I have to help Mr. Bauer then, but I don't want to go to the ball anyway."
"I do—I smelled something delicious cooking," Demi said.
"You know," Tommy said after a moment's thought, "we could leave right after we eat."
"So let's write back and say we'll come," Nat said.
After receiving the boys' note, Daisy was excited, but Nan was concerned.
"Demi and Nat will be good, but Tommy will misbehave," she said, arranging some cupcakes on a plate.
"Then I'll send him right back downstairs!" Daisy said firmly.
Nan nodded. "It's almost three o'clock, and we ought to get dressed," she said.
"Come here, Bess, and I'll tie your apron."
Laurie and Amy's four-year-old daughter was visiting and wanted to play the maid.
Daisy put on a pair of glasses, one of Jo's old shawls, and a nightcap decorated with a red bow.
Nan's outfit included a long skirt, old pink slippers, and a yellow scarf.
Suddenly there was a loud knock at the door, which caused Miss Smith to fly into a chair and fan herself with a feather duster.
Bess answered the door and said, "Come in, gentlemen! Everything's ready!"
In honor of the occasion, the boys wore tall black hats and gloves of every color.
None of them owned a matching pair of gloves.
"Good afternoon, ma'am," Demi said in a deep voice.
Everyone shook hands and then sat down, trying to look like serious adults.
"Oh, stop that!" Mrs. Smith cried as the boys shook with laughter.
"You can't come again, if you act like that!"
Miss Smith hit Tommy with her fan because he was laughing the hardest.
"I can't help it—you both look so funny!"
"So do you, but I wouldn't be rude enough to tell you!"
Mrs. Smith realized that the ball was getting out of control.
"I think we'd better dance now."
"Let's eat first!" Tommy winked at Demi to remind him they could soon leave.
"We never eat first, and if you don't dance nicely, you won't get anything to eat."
Mrs. Smith grabbed Tommy by the hand and announced, "Now I will teach you the polka."
Miss Smith danced with Demi, and Nat played his violin while the two couples danced until they were exhausted.
"You must ask my daughter to play and sing," Mrs. Smith said, flopping into a chair.
"Give us a song, miss," said Demi, wondering where the piano was.
Miss Smith sailed over to an old desk, which she pretended to play.
After far too many songs, Mrs. Smith finally said, "It's time for tea."
Unfortunately, things went wrong right from the beginning of teatime.
The best pie fell on the floor, and the boys gobbled up all the bread and butter.
Miss Smith and the maid fought over the best cupcake, which left the maid in tears.
"Now what's happened to my special tarts?" Mrs. Smith asked.
"I put a raisin on each one and sprinkled them with sugar."
Everyone looked high and low, but the tarts could not be found.
"I know you hid them, Tommy!" the outraged hostess cried.
"Did not!" Tommy said. "Demi stole them."
"What!" Demi cried. "You probably have them in your pockets!"
"Let's take them away from Tommy!" said Nat, surprised at how exciting a ball could be.
Tommy fled behind a table and pelted his friends with the stolen tarts.
When Tommy ran out of tarts to throw, Demi and Nat dragged him into the hall and left him there.
While Demi consoled poor Mrs. Smith and her maid, Nat collected the tarts.
Then Miss Smith replaced the raisins and put a tart on each plate.
"There—good as new!" Miss Smith said.
But no one was interested in eating the tarts after they'd been tossed around the room.
"I guess we'd better go," Demi said suddenly as he heard Jo coming up the stairs.
"Perhaps we should," Nat said, hastily stuffing a cupcake into his pocket.
But Jo arrived before the boys could leave, and the girls poured out their tale of woe.
Jo looked sternly at the boys as she scolded them.
"No more balls until you've made up for your bad behavior by doing something nice for the girls."
Nat and Demi bowed their heads, murmuring, "We're sorry."
"I'm not!" Tommy shouted through the keyhole, where he'd been eavesdropping.
Jo struggled to keep a straight face.
"You may leave, boys, but remember: no talking to or playing with the girls until I give you permission."
The boys ran downstairs as fast as they could.
Tommy pretended not to care and said he could do without "those stupid girls."
Demi and Nat wanted to make up right away, but Daisy and Nan ignored them.
Worst of all, Jo seemed to consider herself one of the offended girls, so she hardly spoke to the boys and had no time for them.
Jo's coldness bothered even Tommy. "We're in real trouble now," he admitted.
For three days Jo and the girls kept their distance from the boys.
Nan took delight in ignoring them, but Daisy didn't like being separated from her twin.
At last the boys couldn't take it anymore and appealed to Mr. Bauer for help.
"To win the girls back, you must do something nice for them," the professor advised.
So Tommy, Nat, and Demi retreated to the attic, where they embarked on a secret project.
Asia grumbled about the amount of paste they were using.
Nan was so curious that she almost got her nose pinched in the attic door while spying.
Meanwhile Daisy lamented that they couldn't all play nicely together.
When the boys were finally ready, Demi marched into Jo's study.
"Please, Aunt Jo, will you and the girls come outside for a party?" he asked.
"Are you sure I won't be in the way?" Jo asked.
"Oh, no!" Demi reassured her.
"The party will be spoiled if you're not there."
Soon Nan, Daisy, and Bess were packed into a wagon drawn by Toby the donkey.
Jo followed behind with Rob and Teddy.
When they came to a hill, they stopped, but there was no sign of a party.
Nan climbed out of the wagon, looking annoyed.
"What's the point of this?" she demanded.
"Hush, Nan!" Jo said, wanting the boys' peace effort to succeed.
But luckily Demi was not discouraged at all.
"If you stand right here," he promised, "a surprise will come to you."
He disappeared behind a large rock, and the girls heard some minor arguing.
"No, you take [i@that@i] one because I'm taking [i@this@i] one," Demi said.
Just when the girls couldn't bear the suspense another moment, the boys appeared.
Each was carrying a new kite, which they presented to Daisy, Nan, and Bess.
The girls shrieked with delight, but Demi silenced them.
"This isn't the whole surprise," he said with a face full of merriment.
The boys disappeared behind the rock and reappeared bearing a giant kite this time.
On it was printed "For Mrs. Bauer" in bright yellow letters.
"We made this for you because you were angry with us and took the girls' side," Nat explained.
"So we owe you an apology too."
All the boys began to shake with laughter because Jo looked so surprised by their gift.
She clapped her hands and joined in the laughter, delighted with their thoughtfulness.
"When we told Uncle Fritz about our plan, he said you'd like a kite too," Demi said.
"He always knows what I like," Jo said with a smile.
"Let's stop talking and fly these kites!" Nan said impatiently.
"I don't know how to—" Daisy began.
"Don't worry, we'll show you what to do," Tommy said.
He rushed to help Nan while Nat, with some effort, persuaded Bess to release her little kite.
Demi was concerned that Jo would feel neglected.
"Let's help Aunt Jo first," he said.
"Hold onto the string, Aunt Jo, and one of us will toss the kite in the air."
"You're very considerate, Demi, but here's a boy who'll help me."
Jo smiled as her husband peeped over the rock.
The professor came out at once and tossed Jo's kite into the air.
She ran off with it, while the children enjoyed the sight of their favorite adult behaving like one of them.
Eventually all the kites soared into the air, where they floated like colorful birds.
Nan raced far across the field, but Bess allowed her kite to go only on short flights.
"Beautiful kite," Bess said, admiring the pictures Tommy had painted on it.
Jo delighted in her giant kite, which seemed as adventurous as its owner.
The kite caught on trees, almost fell into the river, and finally flew so high that it was a mere speck in the sky.
After a while everyone grew tired and fastened the kite strings to a fence.
"Did you ever have such a wonderful time?" Nat asked, lying on the ground and watching the kites fly.
"Not since I last flew a kite years ago when I was a girl," Jo said.
"I wish I had known you then because you must have been so much fun," Tommy said.
Jo laughed and pulled Teddy and Rob onto her lap.
"I might have been fun, but I'm sorry to say I was also a naughty little girl."
"Tell us about the last time you flew a kite," Nat said.
"Uncle Laurie and I were having a grand time flying kites when suddenly we heard voices.
Some people were returning from a picnic, and I was embarrassed to be seen flying a kite at my age.
I was 15, and I knew everyone would laugh at me because my wild ways always amused the neighbors."
"You sound just like Nan!" Tommy said, which earned him a swat from Nan.
"So what happened next?" Demi asked.
"Uncle Laurie took out his pocketknife and cut our kite strings.
Away flew the kites, and when the picnickers arrived, we were picking flowers like proper young people.
After that, I decided to wait until I was an adult before I flew a kite again."
"Then it's a good thing we made one for you!" Tommy said with delight.
Jo nodded in agreement and went over to get her kite from the fence.
"It's almost time for supper."
"Wasn't our party wonderful?" Nat asked Jo and the girls.
"Yes!" the females all cried together.
"And do you know why that was?" Jo asked.
"Because all your guests behaved themselves!"
By July the gardens were thriving, and so were the children, who played outside from morning till night.
One evening when Jo was getting Teddy ready for bed, he pointed excitedly to the window.
"My Danny!" he cried.
"No, honey, he's not there," Jo said, pulling Teddy's nightshirt over his head.
"Danny at the window!" Teddy insisted. "I saw him, Mama!"
"Maybe it was Dan," Jo thought, hurrying to the window.
She called Dan's name, but there was no reply.
"Come, Teddy, help me call Dan."
Jo hoped that Dan might respond to Teddy's voice.
But after a few minutes, both Jo and Teddy were disappointed that Dan did not appear.
After Teddy fell asleep, Jo went downstairs.
She decided her son had been mistaken, so she didn't bother her husband with the news.
While the professor sat in his study, writing letters, Jo mended socks in her study next door.
It was past ten o'clock when Jo rose to shut up the house for the night.
As she paused at a window, something white caught her eye outside.
"Nan has left her hat on one of the haystacks again," she thought.
Jo sighed and went out to retrieve it.
But as she got closer to the haystack, she drew in a breath.
The white object was a shirt—and Dan was lying on the haystack fast asleep!
Ragged, dirty, and thin, he had bandaged one foot with an old jacket while his other foot was bare.
"Dan." Jo bent over Dan and gently called his name.
"I've come home," Dan whispered with a sleepy smile.
"I thought you would return," Jo replied kindly, "and I'm so glad to see you."
At those words Dan's eyes flew open, and he sat up.
His face hardened, and he said rudely, "I'm not staying—I only wanted to peek in as I passed by."
"Why not come in, dear?" Jo said, her face clouding with disappointment.
"Teddy saw you earlier at the window."
"I didn't think you'd let me," Dan said, fumbling for his small bundle, ready to take off.
"Maybe you were mistaken," Jo said, extending one hand to Dan and pointing to the house with the other.
Taking a deep breath, Dan stood up and limped toward the house.
"Mr. Bauer won't be happy when he hears I ran away from Mr. Page's school," he mumbled.
"He already knows, and it won't make any difference to him," Jo said.
"What happened to your foot?"
"When I was climbing over a wall, a heavy stone fell on it, but I don't mind."
Dan did his best to be brave, but Jo could see that every step hurt him.
Once they reached her study, she brought him some food and drink.
"Where have you been, Dan?" she asked.
"Mr. Page was too strict, so I ran off more than a month ago.
I joined a man on a boat, and then I worked for a farmer for a couple of weeks.
But he wouldn't pay me, so I took off again."
"How did you survive?" Jo asked, looking at him with pity in her eyes.
"Folks gave me things to eat," Dan explained, "and I slept in barns."
Jo was still puzzled about his return.
"If you didn't come back to stay with us, why are you here?"
"I wanted to see Teddy again—and you—before I returned to my old job in the city.
I planned to be gone by morning, but you found me."
"Are you sorry I did?" Jo asked, kneeling down to examine his injured foot.
Dan stared at the ceiling and said quietly, "No, I wanted to stay, but I was afraid you—"
"Oh, Dan!" Jo blurted out. "When did you hurt this poor foot?"
"Three days ago."
"Mr. Bauer must look at this at once!"
Jo hurried to her husband's study, leaving the door to her own study ajar.
Dan overheard her telling the professor of his arrival.
"I didn't have the heart to scold him, Fritz, because it's obvious he wants us to take him back," Jo said.
"But he's afraid you won't forgive him."
"This proves we have a hold on the boy's heart. Of course I'll forgive him."
Two tears rolled down Dan's dusty cheeks as he listened, but he quickly wiped them away.
"You must be kind to Dan, no matter how gruff he seems," Jo warned her husband.
"A quiet word and patience will help him, just as they used to help me."
"I doubt you were ever like Dan!" Mr. Bauer said, laughing.
As the Bauers entered Jo's study, Dan tried to stand up but couldn't.
"So you like it here more than at Mr. Page's?" the professor said pleasantly.
"Well, let's see if we can get along better this time."
"Thank you, sir," said Dan, finding it easier to be polite than he'd expected.
After Mr. Bauer bathed and bound up Dan's foot, he said they must call the doctor the next day.
Jo prepared a bed for Dan, who quickly fell asleep.
But he awoke in the middle of the night, moaning in pain.
"Are you all right?" Jo said, arriving at his bedside.
"My foot hurts, but I didn't mean to wake you," Dan said.
"That's all right." Jo smoothed his pillow.
To her great surprise, Dan threw his arms around her neck and kissed her cheek.
"Thank you for taking care of me, ma'am!"
Touched by his words and actions, Jo realized that Dan was sorry.
"You're my boy now," she said, giving him a hug.
The next day was Sunday, and Dr. Firth came to examine Dan's injured foot.
"You must keep Dan quiet for at least a week," Dr. Firth said to Jo.
"After that he may be able to walk with a crutch."
"I will get better, right?" Dan asked anxiously.
"I hope so," Dr. Firth said, returning his instruments to his black bag.
"But remember, absolutely no walking or standing on that foot!"
After the doctor left, Dan shifted uncomfortably in bed.
"What if my foot is like this forever?" he asked Jo.
"I'm famous for my nursing skills, and I won't let that happen."
Jo tried to sound reassuring, though she wasn't confident he'd recover completely.
"Now, would you like some of the boys to visit?"
"Yes, please, Nat and Demi, and I'd like my bundle too, if you haven't thrown it away."
An anxious look crossed Dan's face again.
"I kept it because I could tell it contained something special," Jo said.
She left the room and soon returned with Dan's bundle and the boys.
"Dan, you're back!" Nat said, pleased to see his old friend.
"Whoa! Look at those!" Demi said as Dan unpacked birds' eggs wrapped in moss.
Three black beetles crawled from underneath a smooth stone.
"How did you find all this stuff?"
"Well, you have to know where to look," Dan said.
"When you turn this stone over . . . "
Jo smiled to herself as she slipped away.
"If Dan grows up to be a naturalist and Nat becomes a musician, then I'll have done an excellent job with these two."
Dan's admirers were so fascinated by his stories that they almost missed their Sunday walk.
When Mr. Bauer came to fetch them, Dan looked disappointed.
"Let's move you into the parlor for a change of scenery."
The professor gently picked up Dan, who tried to smile.
After everyone had left, Jo came into the parlor with Teddy and Rob.
"You're a city boy," she said to Dan. "How did you get interested in nature?"
"I didn't know much until I met Mr. Hyde—a naturalist who used to stay at Mr. Page's. Sometimes he'd ask me to assist him with his observations.
Mr. Page thought it was silly, but Mr. Hyde could lie still for hours watching a bird.
He knew so much about everything!" Dan paused for breath.
"I hope I'll get to see him again sometime."
"I hope so too," Jo said, noticing how cheerful Dan had become.
"If you really love those things, I'll make sure you have time to study them."
Dan broke into a wide grin, but his face fell at Jo's next announcement.
"However, you must also work on improving your behavior," she added firmly.
Dan pointed to his injured foot. "How can I possibly do that when I can't even go anywhere?"
"You can be patient and cheerful despite your pain, and you can help me," Jo said.
"You can amuse Rob and Teddy, or wind yarn into balls, or read to me while I sew."
"Yes, ma'am, I'll try to—"
"Dan! Look what I found for you!" Just then Demi raced into the parlor with a toad in each hand.
"I don't think Mrs. Bauer will let me keep those toads in the house."
Dan looked hesitantly at Jo. "Will you?"
Jo laughed and shook her head no.
"If you tell me what to do, I'll take care of them in the barn," Demi offered.
So Dan gave him some instructions, and Demi carried the creatures away.
"Demi cut short his walk to bring me those toads," Dan said, sounding amazed.
"He must have learned how to be nice at home. He's lucky to have parents to help him."
"Yes, my sister Meg and her husband, John, are very kind people.
They've been a good influence on Demi," Jo said, and patted Dan's shoulder.
"And now you have all of us to help you."
Dan spent the next week resting, and on Saturday Dr. Firth declared him well enough to use a crutch.
"Hooray!" Nat rushed off to tell the others.
After lunch Dan limped onto the front porch and sat in a rocker.
Everyone gathered around him to talk and play quiet games.
"Uncle Laurie's here!" Rob suddenly shouted as a carriage came up the drive.
When the carriage stopped in front of the house, Laurie emerged with his daughter, Bess.
Daisy took Bess to her kitchen, and some of the others disappeared to check the gardens and animals.
They wanted everything to look nice for Laurie's inspection.
"I bet you're tired of staying in the house," Laurie said to Dan.
"Oh, yes!" Dan blurted out quickly.
"Then let's take Dan for a drive," Laurie said to Nat. "Go fetch a cushion."
Dan was soon settled in the carriage, his foot resting comfortably upon a cushion.
"I have a book here that you might like." Laurie reached under the seat.
"Mrs. Bauer told me you're interested in nature."
"Wow!" Dan exclaimed as he studied the colorful pictures of birds, butterflies, and other insects.
Nat leaned over Dan's shoulder for a glimpse of the illustrations.
"You know, Mrs. Bauer is very nice," Laurie said.
"But you can't expect her to put up with every creature and nest you boys bring into the house.
This school needs a natural history museum, and I think Dan should be the curator."
Dan hugged the book to his chest with a delighted smile.
"Thank you, sir—that sounds wonderful."
As the carriage ride continued, Dan was still too surprised about the natural history museum to say much, but Nat was eager to discuss it.
"Where will we put the museum?" he asked Laurie.
"In the former carriage house," Laurie replied.
"That gloomy old building?" Nat said.
"There are no windows. Everything's covered with cobwebs, and the roof leaks on rainy days."
Laurie smiled. "You won't recognize the place after Silas and I renovate it.
Mrs. Bauer has already approved my plans, so let's tell everyone else."
Word spread quickly about the museum, and soon everyone gathered in the parlor.
Dan lay on the couch, still clutching his new book.
Laurie sat on a stool at Jo's feet, while the children sprawled on the floor.
"I'm glad you like my idea because I've always wanted to endow an institution," Laurie said to Jo.
"You've been doing that for years," Jo said, gesturing toward the children.
"We can only operate this school because of your financial assistance."
"I know, but I've wanted to do something more," Laurie said.
"Then we'll name this new institution in honor of its founder," Jo said firmly.
"Let's call it The Laurence Museum!"
"Hooray!" everyone shouted together.
Laurie stood up and bowed deeply.
"Founding a museum has made me as hungry as a bear, and that reminds me . . . "
He hurried out to the carriage and returned with a package.
"I almost forgot Grandma March's famous sugar cookies!
She made a special cookie for each of you.
Read her note to figure out which one is yours—I'm pretty sure the bear is for me!"
Everyone laughed as the box was passed around.
Daisy admired her flower cookie before taking a nibble.
"You're lucky Grandma and Grandpa March live with you," she whispered to her cousin Bess.
After the cookies were consumed, it was time for Laurie to inspect the gardens and animals.
When he finished, he stood with Jo outside the barn.
"I always feel refreshed when I visit here.
By the way, how's Nan getting along?"
Jo smiled and patted his arm.
"I know you're not sure about boys and girls going to school together, but Nan's doing quite well.
She's very kind to Bess and Rob, and Daisy is helping her with—"
"Giddyap!"
Jo's remarks were cut short as Nan raced around the corner, driving four "horses."
They were Nat, Tommy, Jack, and Demi tied together with a clothesline.
Nan's make-believe carriage was followed by Daisy pushing Bess in a wheelbarrow.
"Giddyap," Nan cried again.
"Faster! Faster!" Bess shouted to Daisy, who was already running at top speed.
Laurie broke into a grin and nudged Jo. "Or maybe Nan's the one influencing Daisy!"
"Wait and see," Jo whispered as they approached the children.
"Nan will turn out just fine."
"Young ladies, what's going on here?" Laurie asked, plucking Bess from the wheelbarrow.
"We had a race," Nan said, panting, "and I won!"
"I could have run faster, but I was afraid Bess would tumble out," Daisy shouted.
"Go again!" Bess said, wiggling in her father's arms.
"No, my pet," Laurie said, "we need to return home before your mother starts to worry."
As Laurie waved good-bye from the carriage, Jo said, "Give my love to Amy and my parents!"
Then she picked up the wheelbarrow and said to Daisy, "I think it's your turn to ride!"
By the following Saturday, the old carriage house had been transformed into a museum.
A new window let in the sun, and a sign over the door said The Laurence Museum.
All afternoon the boys carried in their treasures and put them on display, according to Dan's instructions.
On one shelf were five different feathers, a snake's skin, and wasps' nest.
There were so many rocks that it was impossible to display them all.
The girls contributed an abundance of dried herbs and flowers.
"I had no idea we'd collected so many interesting things," Jack said, surveying the room.
"If we charged admission, we could make a fortune!"
"Oh no," Laurie said as he came through the door with the Bauers.
"This will always be a free museum, or I'll take my name off the sign."
"That's right," the professor agreed.
"Speech! Speech!" Jo pulled Laurie toward the center of the room.
"As our founder, you must give a speech."
"Let's see . . . ," Laurie said, taking a deep breath.
"You've done a wonderful job with your collections, but donating unusual or pretty things isn't enough.
Once a week you must take turns giving talks about your exhibits."
"That sounds like too much work," Jack grumbled.
But Dan was intrigued by the idea.
"How will we research our talks so they're accurate?"
"Start with your book," Laurie said.
"Jo, do you still have those nonfiction books we used as kids?"
"I think they're in the attic somewhere," she replied.
"Get them out, and I'll provide some more books to complete your library."
"That sounds fabulous!" Jo said.
"Now it's time to wash up for supper, everyone."
The professor herded his students out of the museum.
"I like your plan very much," Jo said to Laurie as they walked along.
"But I'm curious about what inspired this museum."
Laurie stopped and took her hands in his.
"Oh, Jo," he said, "I know what it's like to be a motherless boy.
I can never forget how much you and your family did for me, which is why I want to do the same for your students."
"Where's my hat?" Nan shouted.
"Mrs. Bauer says I can't leave without my hat!"
"Has anybody seen my pail?" Tommy asked.
"It was here a minute ago."
The children were getting ready to pick huckleberries on an August afternoon.
The floor of the hallway was covered with hats, pails, and snacks.
"I can't wait to pick huckleberries!" Rob announced happily as he joined the group.
Jo sighed when she saw her five-year-old son.
"It's much too far for you to walk, Rob.
You'll get so hot and tired that you won't have a good time."
"We're going all the way to the big pasture. We don't want you tagging along," Jack said.
"I can keep up!" Rob insisted.

The sight of Rob's tears touched everyone but Jack, who thought Rob was a nuisance.
"I'll stay home with him," Daisy offered, putting down her pail.
"Oh, let him come," Nan said. "I'll take good care of him."
"I'd carry him if I could," Dan murmured, looking down at his foot.
"But I guess I can't go, even though I'm not using a crutch anymore."
"Thank you for offering, Dan," Jo said, "but you shouldn't overdo things.
Wait a minute, I have an idea." She raced outside.
Silas was driving away in the cart but turned back when he noticed Jo.
A few minutes later she returned to the house, beaming.
"I've arranged things so everyone—including Rob and Dan—can go," Jo explained.
"Silas will drive you to the pasture, and pick you up at five o'clock."
"Hooray!" Rob shouted.
"I won't eat a single berry, Mama—I'll save them all for you!"
Everyone had a delightful afternoon despite some mishaps.
Tommy was stung by a wasp, and Jack fell out of a tree.
Startled by a snake, Daisy dropped her pail and spilled half her berries.
But the boys weren't badly hurt, and Demi helped Daisy refill her pail.
Meanwhile Dan enjoyed himself, observing wild creatures in the grass and sky.
While the others stayed together, Nan wandered off with Rob.
"I keep putting berries in my pail, but it doesn't fill up," Rob complained.
Nan pointed to the woods beyond a stone wall.
"Last time the bushes over there had much bigger berries," she said.

If we went there, we could fill our pails and hide in the cave till everyone found us."
They scrambled over the wall and ran through a field to the woods.
"These bushes do have the best huckleberries!" Rob said as they filled their pails.
"Now we'll find the cave and have something to eat."
"Are you sure you know the way?" Rob asked.
"Of course!" Nan replied, sounding very certain.
"I have an excellent sense of direction—remember when I fetched my suitcase all by myself?"
That convinced Rob, and he followed Nan, who after much meandering, finally located the cave.
They crawled inside to wait for the others.
"Isn't this nice?" Nan said, offering some bread to Rob.
"Yes, but do you think they'll find us soon?" Rob was getting bored and restless.
"No, because when we hear them, we'll stay quiet, and then we'll have fun watching them search for us!"
"What if they don't come?" Rob asked.
"I can find the way home by myself even though it's six miles."
Nan had only a vague idea of distance but a lot of confidence.
After a while Rob said, "I guess we should go now."
"Not until I sort through my berries," Nan said.
Rob tried to wait patiently while Nan slowly examined every berry for flaws.
"Oh no!" he said as the sun dropped behind a hill.
"You said you'd take good care of me, and it's getting dark."
"What?" Startled, Nan looked up from her work.
"We have to get going before they leave without us."
"I heard somebody blowing a horn an hour ago," Rob said, but unfortunately his sense of time was no better than Nan's sense of distance.
"Maybe everybody was searching for us."
"Which direction did the sound come from?" Nan asked.
"Um . . . ," Rob said, hesitating before he pointed. "Over there?"
Nan took off, while Rob tried his best to keep up.
They climbed up and down hills, pausing to listen for the horn.
But they never heard it because it had only been the sound of a cow mooing.
"I don't remember seeing that pile of stones," Nan said as they rested on a wall.
Suddenly her face brightened, and she pointed to something.
"Look—there's the tree that Jack fell from."
But when they reached the tree, it was not the one Jack had climbed.
"Are we lost?" Rob's voice trembled.
"Not really—I just don't see which way to go right now.
If we shout, I'm sure they'll hear us."
The two children shouted until they were hoarse, but no one answered.
"I wish Mama would come find us," Rob said. "Oh, look, there she is!"
Rob ran toward a dim figure slowly approaching them in the dark.
Suddenly he stopped, turned around, and came stumbling back to Nan.
"That's not Mama," he screamed. "It's a bear!"
Although Nan was exceptionally brave, she was afraid of a bear in the dark woods.
That is, until the bear mooed.
When she heard the sound, Nan laughed with relief.
"Oh, Rob, that's not a bear—that's a cow!"
The two children petted the cow until it wandered away.
Nan wanted to resume searching for their friends, but Rob refused to walk.
"It's nighttime and I'm sleepy and I want Mama!" the little boy said.
"Maybe you need a nap," Nan replied.
"Let's sit down, and you can rest your head on my lap."
"Wake me when Mama comes," Rob said, and soon he was asleep.
Nan sat anxiously, hoping that no more animals would emerge from the darkness.
By the time the moon rose, she too had fallen asleep.
While Nan and Rob slept, everyone at Plumfield was in a state of panic.
Dan, Demi, and Daisy had traveled home in the cart with Silas while the other boys had decided to walk home.
When Nat, Tommy, and Jack finally showed up, Jo flew out of her chair.
"Where are Nan and Rob?" she demanded.
"We thought they rode home with Dan and the twins," Nat said.
"We thought [i@you@i] knew where they were!" Demi said.
Now it was Jo's turn to be frightened.
"Find Mr. Bauer and Silas!" she cried.
"Fetch the lanterns, and Jack and Nat, come with me!"
Soon the professor and Silas were on their way to the big pasture.
Without bothering to put on her shawl, Jo rode away on Toby.
"Wait for me!" a voice cried behind her.
As Jo turned around, her lantern revealed Dan hurrying down the drive.
"What are you doing here?" she asked.
"And where are Jack and Nat?"
"I told them I'd accompany you because they hadn't eaten any supper yet," Dan said.
"Besides, I wanted to come more than they did."
"If you insist on helping, then you have to ride Toby," Jo said, jumping off the donkey and handing the reins to Dan.
But Dan wouldn't take them. "I couldn't, ma'am," he said, "because you—"
"You're no use to us if you make your foot worse with too much walking," Jo reminded him.
Reluctantly Dan climbed onto Toby and set off with Jo walking beside him.
"Nan! Rob!" Periodically they stopped and called for the children, but no little voices replied.
When they arrived at the big pasture, they saw lanterns flitting here and there.
The professor shouted, "Nan! Rob! Rob! Nan!" while Silas whistled and yelled.
"Hush, everyone!" Jo said with a sob in her voice.
"You're frightening them with all this noise.
Rob will recognize my voice, so let me call. Nan! Rob!"
Over and over she called with no response.
The sky was overcast now, and the moon made only brief appearances from behind the clouds.
A far-off rumble of thunder indicated that a summer storm was brewing.
Jo wandered through the field like a pale ghost.
"Oh, my poor Rob! And if Nan's been harmed, how will I ever explain it to her father?
Oh, Rob, where are you?"
Dan could not take Jo's despair for another moment.
He dismounted and tied Toby to a fence.
"Maybe they went into the woods," he said.
Then he climbed over the wall before Jo could stop him.
"I see footprints!" he cried a moment later. "Come here!"
Jo was the first to reach Dan, who was shining a lantern on the ground.
"Yes!" she cried joyfully. "Those are tracks from Rob's boots!"
A little farther on, they found Nan's hat, and they soon came upon the two children, both sound asleep.
"Rob!" Jo cried, sweeping him into her arms.
"Mama! I knew you'd come!"
Rob clutched his pail of berries, which was still full. "Look at all the berries I picked for you!"
Meanwhile Dan gently picked up Nan, who began to cry.
"My poor little girl, don't cry!" Jo said.
"You're safe now, and we won't ask for any explanations tonight."
But Nan's apology came tumbling out.
"It's all my fault. I tried my best to take care of Rob, and I let him sleep, and I didn't eat any of his berries, even though I was so hungry.
I'll never do it again, I promise and . . . " She dissolved in tears, relieved to be rescued.
After a happy reunion with the professor and Silas, the group set out for home.
Daisy and the boys were still awake, and they joyfully greeted Rob and Nan.
"It's almost 11 o'clock," the professor said when the wanderers had finished a late supper.
"Time for bed, everyone."
"Thank goodness there won't be any empty beds tonight," Jo said, her eyes filling with tears.
While Daisy escorted Nan to bed, the professor carried Rob upstairs.
"Poor Aunt Jo is so tired, she should be carried upstairs too," Demi said.
"Let's do that!" Tommy shouted.
"No, thank you!" Jo said, fearing Tommy might drop her.
"But someone may lend me an arm to lean on."
"Me! Me! Me!" The boys jostled each other, eager to be chosen.
Jo smiled at Dan and said, "You found the children, so you must be given the honor."
Dan proudly escorted her upstairs.
When they reached Jo's door, she turned and said, "God bless you, my boy."
Dan hesitated and then said softly, "I wish I really were your boy."
"I will always think of you as my oldest son," Jo said, kissing his cheek.
And that was more than enough to satisfy Dan.
After Nan and Rob's misadventure, Jo hoped for some quiet, trouble-free days.
And things did remain peaceful until Tommy's hens caused a problem.
Tommy had been steadily earning money from selling their eggs.
But he spent his money so recklessly that Mr. Bauer insisted he start saving it.
The professor gave Tommy a bank that was shaped like a miniature house.
"After you've saved five dollars, you may open the bank, but you must spend the money wisely."
Tommy soon had four dollars in the bank, which he kept under his bed.
When Jo paid him another dollar for eggs, Tommy rushed to the barn to show Nat.
"Look at these!" Tommy said, displaying four quarters.
"Oh, I wish I had that dollar."
Nat was still Tommy's partner in the egg business, but he always had fewer eggs to sell than Tommy.
"I'd add it to the money I'm saving for a violin."
"I have five dollars now, but I haven't decided how to spend it."
Tommy tossed the shiny quarters in the air and caught them.
"Maybe I'll lend you some."
"Hey, everybody!" a voice called from outside the barn.
"Dan just caught a huge snake!"
"Come on, let's go!"
Tommy was in too much of a hurry to put his money in his bank, so he hid the quarters under an old feed sack in the barn.
The interesting snake made Tommy forget about his quarters until bedtime.
"I'll get them tomorrow," he said to himself.
"Nobody except Nat knows where they're hidden anyway."

"What are you talking about?" Demi asked.
Tommy described how he'd hidden the quarters under the old feed sack.
"That's right," Nat said. "I saw him do it."
"Somebody must have stolen the money," Jack said.
"When I find out who did it," Tommy said, "I'll—"
"Stay calm," Dan interrupted.
"We'll figure this out because thieves usually give themselves away."
"What's all this about thieves?" the professor asked, coming into the schoolroom.
Tommy explained the situation again.
When he reached the part about hiding the money, everyone looked at Nat.
"I know you think I stole it, but I didn't!" Nat cried, his face turning red.
"Take your seats," Mr. Bauer said.
"I'm going to ask each of you a question, and I want an honest answer.
Don't make things worse for yourself by lying."

Finally it was Nat's turn.
"Now, my boy, please give me an honest answer," the professor said.
"Did you take the money?"
"No, sir."
Nat looked so miserable that the professor felt some compassion for him.
But Mr. Bauer also knew that Nat had a history of lying, especially to keep himself out of trouble.
"I'm very sorry, Nat, but the evidence is against you," the professor said gravely.
"And the lies you've told in the past cause me to doubt you now.
I'll give you another chance to tell the truth, if you want one.
That's up to you and your conscience."

He hung his head in shame because he couldn't bear to look at his friends.

Jo was as kind as ever, but she seemed disappointed in him.
And the sad look in the professor's eyes broke Nat's heart because he loved his teacher dearly.
One person who still believed in Nat was Daisy.
When Nat played his fiddle, Daisy sat by his side.
She made him special treats in her kitchen and brought him flowers from her garden.
Dan also jumped to Nat's defense whenever anyone criticized him.
After a while some of the boys began to doubt that Nat had taken the money.
A rumor started circulating that Dan was behind the theft.
One afternoon Nat encountered Dan watching insects gliding over the surface of the brook.
"Thanks for sticking up for me," Nat said to his old friend.
"I'm sorry that some people are accusing you of being the thief."
Dan turned away from Nat, tossing a stone into the brook.
"How do you know they're not right?"
"Because you don't care about money!" Nat said fiercely.
"All you're interested in are bugs and rocks and things."
"I want a butterfly net as much as you want a fiddle," Dan said.
"Why wouldn't I steal the money for it?"
"You like to fight sometimes, but I don't believe you'd lie or steal."
"Well, I've done both," Dan said, throwing another stone into the water.
"I used to lie all the time, and I stole things to eat when I ran away from Mr. Page."
"Oh, Dan, tell me it's not you!" Nat said in distress.
"It's not me," Dan replied.
"But don't worry—we'll figure out who the real culprit is."
Nat studied Dan's face and said slowly, "I think you already know who it is.
If you do, beg him to tell the truth because I don't think I can stand this much longer.
If I were as brave as you are, I'd run away.
But I'm not, so I have to wait for someone to tell the truth."
"You won't have to wait much longer," Dan said, and then he quickly walked away and wasn't seen for hours.
Over the next few days, Dan was moodier than usual.
As for Tommy, he cut Nat out of his egg business.
"I can't trust you anymore," Tommy said.
"But I didn't take your money!" Nat protested.
Tommy scrubbed "Tommy Bangs & Company" from the barn wall.
"And don't go stealing any of my eggs!"
"I wouldn't! Tommy, wait . . . ," Nat called after his friend as he ran from the barn.

"Those stupid hens have moved their nests, and I can't find any eggs!" he complained loudly.
"At least the hens trusted [i@me@i]," Nat said to himself.
"Tommy, come quick!" Demi shouted. "Look what I found!"
Tommy ran to where Demi was pointing to a paper on the floor.
Next to the words "For Tommy Bangs" were four quarters.
Tommy's eyes widened in surprise.
"Where did those come from?"
Demi glanced at Nat. "The thief must have put them there."
Nat was tired of being a suspect.
"How could I do that when I didn't take them in the first place?"
Dan wandered over to see what was happening.
"It doesn't matter who took them.
What's important is that everyone can be friends with Nat again."
That night at supper, Mr. Bauer found a package on his chair with a note attached.
While the professor read the note, Demi ripped open the package.
"This is the book Uncle Laurie gave Dan!"
Demi held up the book for all to see, while Dan turned red and stared at the table.
"What does the note say, dear?" Jo asked.
"Our neighbor Mrs. Bates was concerned because her son purchased this book from Dan for a dollar," the professor said.
"She's returning it because she thinks it's worth more than that.
Did you sell your book, Dan?"
"Yes, sir," Dan said slowly. "I owed somebody some money."
"Who?" the professor asked.
"Tommy."
"Did you put those quarters in the barn this morning?"
Dan looked Mr. Bauer in the eye. "Yes, I did."
Tommy dropped his mug with a crash while Daisy said, "I knew Nat wasn't the thief!"
Jo left the room looking so disappointed that Dan couldn't bear it.
He hid his face in his hands for a moment and then looked up defiantly.

Dan shoved the table as he pushed back his chair. "I'm not sorry!" he cried, fleeing the room.
"At least we know you didn't do it," the professor said to Nat.
"I apologize for doubting that you told the truth."
"I'm sorry too," Tommy said to Nat.
"Do you want to be partners in the egg business again?"
Nat nodded but said sorrowfully, "I wish the thief was anybody but Dan."
Days passed, and Dan went about his work, silent, grim, and unrepentant.
"The theft was bad enough," Jo said to her husband, "but to lie about it and then let Nat take the consequences.
That was even worse!"
"I agree," the professor said.
"And Dan has stubbornly refused to talk about it or apologize."
"I had such high hopes for Dan, but now . . . " Jo's voice trailed off, and she looked worried and sad.
That afternoon Dan came upon the other boys playing in the birch grove.
They were climbing a birch tree, grabbing slender, bendable branches, and swinging down to the ground.
Dan stopped to watch as Jack took his turn.
Unfortunately Jack had chosen to climb out on a high, thick branch—too thick to bend or swing.
Now he was stuck there, dangling from a dangerous height.
"You're going to fall!" Tommy cried from the ground. "Go back!"
Jack tried to do that, but his hands kept slipping.
"I can't hold on much longer!"
Demi's face was white with fear. "You'll get killed if you fall!"
"I'll help you!" Dan scrambled up the tree and was soon dangling from Jack's branch.
Dan's weight bent the branch, and Jack dropped safely to the ground.
But the branch flew up so suddenly that Dan lost his grip and fell.
Pale and dizzy, he sat up slowly, while the boys gathered around him in admiration.
"You saved my life!" Jack said.
"It was nothing," Dan muttered, brushing himself off and walking slowly away.
The next morning Mr. Bauer bounded into the schoolroom and practically shouted, "Dan is not the thief!"
He shook Dan's hand and apologized.
Tommy looked puzzled, asking, "Then who is?"
The professor pointed to an empty seat.
"Jack went home early this morning, but he left me a note confessing to the crime.
He was peeking through a crack in the barn when he saw Tommy hide the money.
After Dan saved his life, Jack couldn't stay silent any longer."
Nat went over and stood by his old friend.
"Dan, I don't understand why you said you took the money."
"I knew you weren't the thief, and I didn't like the way everyone was blaming you."
Dan turned to the professor.
"I'm sorry I lied, sir, but I did it for my friend. Does Mrs. Bauer know the truth?"
"Yes!" Jo said from the doorway, looking ready to dance for joy.
"Three cheers for Dan!"
After washing some doll clothes, Nan and Daisy spread them to dry on the grass.
"Let's climb the willow tree," Nan said.
"We can keep an eye on the clothes so they don't blow away."
That summer the old willow tree had become a favorite spot for everyone to sit and chat.
"I hate washing clothes!" Nan said as she settled onto a branch.
"Oh, I don't mind washing at all," Daisy said.
"I like cooking and cleaning and anything that has to do with keeping house.
When I grow up, I'll have a nice house where Demi and I can live together."

"I'll have an office, where I can work as a doctor.
And when my patients are too sick to visit, I'll make house calls.
Curing folks is my idea of fun—not housekeeping!"
