She was smart, brave, and felt compassion for anyone sick or in pain.
Jo let Nan assist her whenever any of the boys needed bandaging.
She planned to keep encouraging Nan and her plan to study medicine.
Daisy was still thinking of the more unpleasant aspects of a doctor's life.
"Will you cut off legs and pull out teeth?"
Nan nodded. "I'll do all those things.
My grandpa was a doctor, and I watched him sew a cut on a man's face.

"I feel sorry for sick people and want to help them, but I shake at the sight of blood."

"I have a splinter in my finger."

"Will one of these work?" she asked.

"No thanks!" Daisy said, turning her head until Nan had finished removing the splinter.

"Thanks, Nan!" Tommy said.
"Do you mind if I sit here a minute with you—I'm waiting for Nat."
Nan moved over to make more room for Tommy.
"Hey, Daisy!" Nat called from below.
"Your doll clothes are blowing away!"

"But won't it be expensive?"
"Of course it will, but so far everyone I've asked has contributed.

"From now on, I'm going to give away my cash as fast as I earn it.

"But I thought Mr. Bauer wanted you to [i@save@i] your money."

It was so quiet and peaceful in the tree that Nat wished he'd brought along his violin.
And that soon gave him an idea.
"You know, I don't really need a new violin," Nat said.
"I could buy Dan a butterfly net, and if there's any money left over, I could donate it to the microscope fund."

"Let's ask Mr. Bauer if we can go into town together on Monday afternoon.

The willow tree soon had a new pair of visitors: Demi and Dan, who'd been collecting leaves.
"Let's sort our leaves," Demi said, climbing into the tree.
Dan held up two different leaves and sighed.
"If only I had a microscope, I could show you some interesting things."
"You'll soon—um . . . " Demi caught himself before he revealed the secret.
"Uh . . . look over there!"
Jo was reading a book as she walked along with Teddy trotting behind her.
"I wonder how long before they notice us," Dan whispered.
Both boys sat completely still as Jo and Teddy approached.
Jo was so absorbed in her book—which she'd been trying to read all week—that she almost wandered into the brook.
Fortunately Teddy interrupted her reading in the nick of time.
"Mama, I want to fish!" Teddy said, tugging on his mother's sleeve.
"You'll need a fishing pole," Jo replied.
Before she could look for a suitable stick, a willow bough fell at her feet.
Looking up, she saw the boys laughing in their secret hideaway.
"I want to climb up there!" Teddy said.
"I'll come down, and then you can come up," Demi said.
"I need to find Daisy anyway."
Leaning down, Dan scooped up Teddy and then offered Jo his hand.
"There's plenty of room for you too, Mrs. Bauer."
A moment later Jo was enjoying a shady seat.
"I haven't climbed a tree since I was married," she said, looking pleased with herself.
"When I was a girl, I was quite fond of climbing trees."
"Now you can read if you want, and I'll take care of Teddy," Dan said,
pulling some string and a pin from his pocket so he could make a fishing rod.
"What were you and Demi doing up here?" Jo asked.
"Just talking about the leaves we found."
Dan bent the pin into a hook and handed the fishing rod to Teddy.
He wrapped an arm protectively around Teddy, so the little boy wouldn't fall.
"I'm glad you're taking the time to talk to Demi," Jo said.
"He thinks you're the bravest boy in the world."
"I didn't know if you'd trust me with him," Dan replied.

"Well, Demi is so kind and good . . . ," Dan began.
"Yes, he's just like his father, John."

"You're not a bad influence!" Jo said loudly, "and I do trust—"
"Shh, Mama, you'll scare the fish!" Teddy interrupted.
Jo continued in a hushed voice.
"I do trust you, Dan. Not only with Demi, but with my own sons.

That's something he can't get from books, no matter how many stories he reads.
Meanwhile he can improve your sense of right and wrong."

No one had ever trusted him or taken the time to discover the good in him.
He felt he had friends now and a place in the world, as well as something to live for.
"Thank you, ma'am" was all he could say.
Suddenly Teddy shouted, "A fish—I caught a fish!"
Dan helped Teddy pull in his catch and then asked, "Do you know what kind of fish this is? A trout!
I've never even seen one here before—good job!"
The three of them went back to the house to show off Teddy's fine catch before Asia cooked it for supper.
For a few hours, the seat in the willow tree remained empty.
But around sunset a boy sneaked up the drive, across the lawn, and into the tree.
Jack was trying to decide what to do next when Mr. Bauer appeared below on his evening walk.
Jack took a deep breath and called out to him. "Hi, Mr. Bauer."
"I'm glad to see you, Jack," the professor said, looking up.
"I didn't want to come back," Jack blurted out, "but my uncle made me because this school is the cheapest one around.
He punished me pretty hard." Jack kicked nervously at the tree trunk.
"Are you going to punish me, Mr. Bauer? Is everyone still mad at me?"
"I can't predict how the boys will react.
But since Dan and Nat suffered so much punishment without doing anything wrong, you should probably suffer some consequences too."
"I returned Tommy's dollar, and I said I was sorry in my note to you. Isn't that enough?"
"No, you should apologize to the three boys," the professor said.
Jack didn't feel brave enough for that.
"What if I auction off some of my things?" he asked.
The professor understood how much money meant to Jack.
"First, it would be better to give away your things than to make money from them.
Second, your friends would value your apology more than your things.
You should think about what's more important to you—money or friends."
Jack watched the willow branches sway in the breeze.
"Okay, fine," he muttered. "I'll apologize."
So Jack climbed down from the tree, and, with the professor's help, he took his first steps back into the Plumfield family.
Jo stood at the parlor window watching Dan.
He ran up and down the drive, leaping and turning somersaults.
"Are you training for a race?" Jo called out.
Dan walked over to the window.
"No, I'm only . . . " He stopped to catch his breath.
"I'm only working off my excess energy so I don't run away from here."
He quickly corrected himself.
"I mean, I'm grateful for all you've done, but sometimes . . . "
"When I was your age, I almost ran away from home myself," Jo said with an understanding smile.
"Run away if you must, Dan, but come back soon because I'll miss you."
Dan was surprised by this unexpected permission.
"Well, I guess I won't go just yet."
"Good! Now let's think of another activity for you." Jo paused, deep in thought for a moment.
"I know—how about driving into town every day before school to do my errands?"
"Really?" Dan said excitedly. "You'd trust me with a horse and wagon?"
"Of course. You're good with animals."
So the next morning Dan took on his new responsibility.
He was happy for a while, but a few weeks later, Mr. Bauer caught him fighting with Jack.
"You know fighting is forbidden!" the professor said sternly, separating the boys.
"We were just wrestling," Dan said to Mr. Bauer, but then he apologized to Jack.
"You need another outlet for your energy, Dan," the professor said, "so come with me."
Mr. Bauer took him to a place where several huge trees had fallen in a storm.
Soon Dan was busy chopping wood, and the professor was explaining Dan's newest chore to Jo.
"When he gets bored with that," Jo said, "I don't know what we'll do."
But Jo didn't need to worry because Dan soon found something to amuse himself.
One afternoon Laurie brought a young horse called Prince Charlie to board at Plumfield.
At first all the boys were fascinated by the handsome creature galloping around the pasture.
But eventually everyone grew tired of watching Charlie—that is, everyone but Dan, who visited Charlie every day with an apple.
No matter where Charlie was in the wide pasture, he came running when Dan whistled.
"We understand each other, don't we, fella?" Dan said, rubbing the horse's nose.
Laurie often came to see how Charlie was getting along.
"I'm thinking of trying to ride him," he said to Dan during one visit.
"He's young, but I don't think it will take much work to tame him."
"He lets me lead him, but I don't think he'll tolerate anyone putting a saddle on him," Dan replied.
"Oh, I'll tumble off at first, but Charlie will quickly get used to a rider."
As Laurie walked away, Dan found himself staring at the horse.
"Hmm. I wonder what Charlie [i@would@i] do if somebody tried to ride him," he thought.
The longer Dan studied Charlie, the more obsessed he became with riding the horse.
Sitting on the fence one day, Dan held out an apple.
As Charlie nibbled away, Dan quietly slipped onto the horse's back.
With an astonished snort, Charlie reared and threw Dan to the ground.
The fall didn't hurt Dan, who jumped up and laughed.
"Come here, Charlie, and let's try that again!"
But Charlie refused to approach him.
"I'll ride you yet!" Dan vowed.
This was exactly the kind of challenge that appealed to him.
The next day Dan tried again.
The horse tried to buck Dan off, but Dan held on until Charlie started galloping.
This time Dan landed hard on the ground.
He lay still while Charlie tore around the field.
After a few minutes, the horse cautiously approached Dan.
Charlie sniffed the boy, who looked up and said, "You think you've beaten me, but you're mistaken."
The following day Dan strapped a folded blanket to Charlie's back and let him race and rear.
After a few more days, Dan was able to sit on Charlie.
Every day after that, he managed a short ride before Charlie threw him.
"I wish I could try a real saddle and bridle on you," Dan said, "but I'm afraid to tell anyone that I've been riding you."
Little did Dan realize that Silas had been watching them.
"Do you know that Dan's been trying to ride Mr. Laurence's horse?" Silas asked Mr. Bauer that evening.
"He kept coming back from the pasture all black and blue. So I figured I'd keep an eye on him."
"What?" Mr. Bauer said. "That sounds dangerous—you should have stopped him, Silas!"
"But he was making progress with that horse. You should see them together."
When the professor and Laurie confronted Dan, he confessed at once.
Then he proudly showed them what he had accomplished with Charlie.
"Thanks to your patience and perseverance, Charlie looks ready for a saddle," Laurie said to Dan.
"Let me train him some more, and then you may ride him whenever you want."
The other boys were jealous that Dan had made a pet of Charlie, but Jo admired what he'd done.
She liked to lean on the fence and watch him work with the horse.
"Charlie's a much nicer animal than the one who used to run wild," Jo said.
"I'm taming a young horse myself, and I hope I'll succeed one day too."
Dan laughed because he realized she was talking about him.
Giving the horse a pat, he said, "We won't jump over the fence and run away, will we, Charlie?"
Every Wednesday afternoon the students assembled at the Laurence Museum for lectures on natural history.
This week Nan, Daisy, and Nat were the speakers.
Nan went first, and her subject was the sponge.
"The sponge is an interesting animal," she began.
"For example, you can wash your face with it.
Some people don't use a sponge, and they are dirty."
Here Nan looked at Tommy, who glared back at her.
"You can also use a sponge to wake up people, especially boys.
If a boy refuses to get up in the morning, stand over his head and squeeze water from a sponge onto his face.
He'll wake up fast!"
Everyone burst into laughter except for Tommy.
"You're wandering off topic," he said.
"I want to know what a sponge eats and where it lives."
"I'll get to that, if you stop interrupting!"
Nan shook her finger at him and went on to tell about the life of a sponge.
She finished her lecture to lots of applause.
The next speaker was Daisy, who cleared her throat nervously.
"My topic is the cat," she began.
"Cats are sweet animals, and I love them very much because they are clean and pretty, and they catch rats and mice.
Some cats can even catch fish!"
"So can I!" Teddy jumped up from Jo's lap, eager to talk about the trout he'd caught.
"Hush, dear," Jo said as she settled him down again. "Let Daisy speak."
"I have a cat named Topaz," Daisy continued, "and I named her that because she has yellow eyes.
Topaz is a gem that is sometimes yellow, though it can be blue or brown or other colors.
I heard about a cat that liked to fish, so I tried that with Topaz."
Daisy took a deep breath before going on.
"But Topaz didn't like the water, and she scratched me.
She might like tea though, because whenever I play in my kitchen, she pats the teapot with her paw. The end."
"That was a good report!" Nat called out as Daisy returned to her seat.
Then he stood up and walked slowly to the front of the room.
"I read about owls in Dan's book," Nat said.
"Owls have big heads, round eyes, hooked bills, and strong claws.
They all fly quietly and hunt their prey at night, yet different owls make different sounds."
Nat began hooting like an owl.
Something moved under his jacket, and he patted it gently.
"After eating, owls spit up the parts they can't digest."
"Ew!" Daisy said.
But Nan leaned forward, full of curiosity. "Like what parts?"
"Bones, feathers, fur," Nat said.
"They spit up things called owl pellets. And now I want to show you something."
He reached under his jacket and pulled out a small, sleepy owl.
"Ohh!" the children cried loudly.
The owl suddenly flew into the rafters, where it sat staring down at them.
"Well . . . ," Nat said, looking up at the bird and then scratching his head.
"I guess that's the end of my speech."
"Very good, Nat," the professor said.
"I trust your feathered friend will fly home if we prop open the museum door?"
Nat nodded.
"Then I think we're finished for today," Mr. Bauer said.
"No, we're not! We still have the . . . the . . . thing!"
Tommy said, trying not to spill the secret.
"Oh, right!" The professor sat down again as Tommy went outside.
Tommy returned, carrying Jo's best silver tray with a red box upon it.
Escorted by Nat and Demi, he marched up to Dan.
Tommy had prepared a magnificent speech, but at that moment, he couldn't remember any of it.
"Here!" Tommy thrust the present toward Dan.
"We . . . er, respect you and want to make up for treating you so badly, so take this and have fun with it!"
Startled, Dan turned as red as the box.
He blurted out an awkward "thanks" as he fumbled with the box.
But when Dan saw what was inside, his face lit up.
"A microscope!" Dan cried, holding up his new treasure so everyone could admire it.
"Just what I've always wanted, and it's a beauty!"
Pleased with the success of their surprise, the boys crowded around Dan to shake his hand.
Jo and the professor stood outside the circle, enjoying the happy scene.
Jack hung back too, aware that his theft of Tommy's money had caused all the trouble.
But soon the professor nudged him forward.
"Go on, shake hands, Jack," Mr. Bauer said. "Everything's forgiven now."
After Dan had finished thanking his friends, he made his way over to the Bauers.
He extended his hand, first to the professor, and then to Jo.
"This was your idea, Mrs. Bauer, wasn't it?" he asked.
"I had nothing to do with it," Jo said with a grin.
"The boys thought this up by themselves."
Teddy reached up to hug Dan. "My good Danny—everybody loves him now."
"Come on, Dan, show us some tadpoles or bugs," Jack said, forgetting his embarrassment.
Dan placed an insect under the microscope and then beckoned to Jack, who peered through the lens.
"Look at the claws on that thing!" Jack said.
"Let me see!" Nan said, pushing her way to the front of the line.
Everyone took a turn, and then Dan showed them a moth wing, some dog hair, and a cobweb.
All these wonders were greeted with exclamations of delight.
"Dan can show you many miracles," Mr. Bauer said. "He's a magician now."
"Dan is more than that," Jo said. "He's our new professor of natural history!"
In September the children harvested their Plumfield gardens, and what a bountiful harvest it was!
Demi was able to send boxes of turnips to his grandparents, while Jack had so much corn and potatoes, he was thinking of selling them.
"I'll be glad to buy your potatoes because we go through pounds of that vegetable every week!" Mr. Bauer said.
Daisy's garden had bloomed from spring to fall, and she regularly sent bouquets to her parents, Meg and John Brookes.
No matter the weather, she faithfully tended her roses, zinnias, and other flowers.
Rob had grown four small squash and one gigantic pumpkin, which was so large two small children could sit on it.
Not that he let anyone sit on it! Instead Rob babied the giant fruit, protecting it from the frost with an old quilt.
"Your pumpkin will provide us with plenty of Thanksgiving pies," Jo said.
"I can think of another use for it too, but that's a surprise."
Nan had grown herbs, and her garden had bloomed with useful plants.
Now she was busy cutting and drying her harvest.
She also kept a little book, where she wrote down the uses for different herbs.
"I don't want to poison one of my patients with the wrong herb!" she said.
Meanwhile Tommy had neglected the beans he'd planted.
When rain was scarce, he hadn't watered them, and then he'd let weeds and pests overtake them.
By midsummer his bean crop had failed.
He'd next planted peas, but it was too late in the season for them to grow.
All he succeeded in growing were thistles, which Toby, the donkey, liked to eat.
"Next year I'm just going to grow thistles for Toby," Tommy announced.
In contrast, Nat had a bumper crop of beans.
"What a lot of beans you've grown!" Jo said, admiring his overflowing baskets.
"This was my first garden, and I planted too many beans," Nat said, shaking his head.
"It's going to take me forever to shell all of them!"
"Hmm . . . leave it to me," Jo said with a smile.
Later that day a notice appeared on the barn door, inviting everyone to a dance on Saturday night.
"'Casual attire,'" Nan read the words aloud, "'and take off your shoes at the door.'"
Daisy studied the sign with a disappointed expression.
"I guess that means we can't wear our best dresses," she said.
But her face brightened as she read the rest of the notice.
"Oh, it says Nat is going to play his violin!"
On Saturday night the barn floor was covered with Nat's beans.
"Come on in, everybody!" he called to his friends, who were taking off their shoes.
"Mrs. Bauer came up with a great idea for shelling my beans.
All you have to do is dance on the pods, and the beans will be shelled—ready?"
The children laughed, and Nat began to play.
The beans were quickly shelled, and everyone helped Nat discard the pods.
Then they danced until it was time for bed.
The only person who did not have a garden was Dan because he'd been away for much of the summer.
When the others harvested their crops, he looked sad that he had nothing to offer.
But as autumn went on, he thought of a different kind of harvest.
Every Saturday he went off to the forests, fields, and hills and returned with armloads of treasures.
"You bring the woods to me!" said Jo, who now spent her Saturday afternoons arranging Dan's colorful leaves, grasses, and berries.
"I hope you don't mind, but I put some nuts in the attic," Dan said.
"There are walnuts, chestnuts, and hazelnuts, all in separate boxes that cover half the attic floor."
"Nan's herbs are up there too, hanging to dry.
And Jack is storing corn for popping, while Daisy is putting packets of flower seeds in an old dresser."
Jo laughed. "We have plenty to be thankful for in the attic, and it's not even Thanksgiving yet!"
Dan was not the only one gathering nuts.
A huge butternut tree grew on the property, and Mr. Bauer had promised the nuts to Rob and Teddy.
"I'm going to pick the most nuts!" Teddy said one day as he worked.
But he soon grew tired and left his basket on the lawn.
"Have you and Teddy given up?" Silas asked Rob a few days later.
"The squirrels are busy gathering nuts, and they won't leave you any."
"Oh, Silas, there are plenty of nuts for us," Rob said.
Silas shook his head as he said, "Most of them have fallen, and the squirrels have carried them away."
Rob was alarmed to see that Silas was right.
"Come on, Teddy—we have to pick nuts right now."
The boys worked hard all afternoon while the squirrels chattered at them from the tree.
Right before supper they put the last of the nuts in a little shed.
"There, we're done!" Rob said.
But the squirrels had not given up.
The next day Silas took the boys out to the shed.
"I noticed your squirrel friends kept dropping onto the roof and disappearing," Silas said.
"Then I saw one poke its head out of a hole—it was carrying one of your nuts."
"They're not squirrel [i@friends@i]!" Rob cried. "They're squirrel [i@thieves@i]!"
"I'll help you move the nuts," Silas said, "but you need a better hiding place."
"Up in the attic!" Teddy said. "That's where my Danny stores his nuts!"
"Wake up, Demi!" Jo said softly.
"I need you to get up right now."
"I just went to bed," Demi said in a sleepy voice, "so it can't be morning yet."
"You're right, but your father is ill, and we must go to him," Jo said, beginning to sob.
"My poor John!"
Suddenly Demi was aware that something was terribly wrong.
No one ever called him John—a name he shared with his father.
"Is Papa very sick?" he asked.
Jo swallowed hard and said, "We're going to say good-bye to him.
Get dressed quickly, and come to my study. I must wake Daisy."
As he dressed, Demi sensed that his world was about to change.
Daisy was soon ready, and the twins got into the carriage with Jo and the professor.
All the way into town, Daisy and Demi held hands.
The next morning breakfast was a dismal meal without Jo at the table.
When it was time for school, the professor's chair was empty too.
"What are we supposed to do today?" Jack asked in confusion.
"I don't feel like playing," Tommy said, and the others agreed.
"Let's try to do our lessons as usual," Dan suggested.
"That'll make the day go faster and please the professor."
"But who will be the teacher?" Nan asked.
"I'll teach you about wolves and foxes," Dan said, "and then maybe you could read quietly while I take Teddy outside to play."
And that's what the children were doing when the professor returned home later in the morning.
The children knew at once from his expression that John Brookes had died.
"Don't cry, Papa!" Rob said, running to his father.
"We've been doing our lessons!" Tommy said.
"Thank you, everyone." Mr. Bauer scooped Rob into his arms.
"You've made a hard day easier. Unfortunately, I must return to town soon."
"When will Mama come home?" Rob asked.
"Tonight," the professor said, kissing his son.
"Right now Aunt Meg needs her."
"Teddy's been crying for her, and he slapped Asia and was terribly naughty!"
Rob reported, hoping that news would bring his mother home immediately.
But it did not.
Professor Bauer left again, and for the rest of the day, the house was very still, like a Sunday.
Nan and the boys spent their time walking, sitting in the willow tree, and tending to their pets.
At dusk Jo and the professor returned home, but Demi and Daisy had stayed in town with their mother.
"Where's my baby?" an exhausted Jo said upon entering the house.
"Here!" Teddy cried. "My Danny took care of me all day, and I was good!"
Jo turned to thank Dan, but he was whispering to the others, "Don't bother her right now."
"No, children, please don't stay away from me," Jo said with a tired smile.
"I've neglected you all day, so I'll rest with Teddy in my study, while you bring me my supper on a tray."
There was a general stampede into the dining room, where everyone fought for the honor of bringing Jo some food.
"Calm yourselves!" the professor said.
"Half of you can bring her supper, while the rest can clear the dishes away."
Another mother might have found it annoying to have children upsetting cups and rattling spoons while they tried to be quiet.
But that night Jo felt especially fond of the children, touched by their concern for her.
Several of them lacked mothers or fathers or both, which made their efforts even more endearing.
When Jo's tray had been removed, Dan offered to put Teddy to bed.
"I wish I could do something helpful," Nat said with a sigh.
"You can, dear," said Jo.
"Get your violin and play some of the sweet songs that Uncle Laurie sent last week."
As Jo listened, she fell asleep in her chair and forgot her sorrow for an hour.
A few days later, the children went into town for John Brookes' funeral.
Everyone was there—Mr. and Mrs. March, Uncle Laurie and Aunt Amy, old Mr. Laurence, and a few friends.
Mr. March conducted the simple service at Meg's house, and the boys did their part by singing a hymn.
That evening at Plumfield, everyone sat in the schoolroom, talking of John Brookes.
"He wasn't a rich man, was he?" Jack asked.
"No," Tommy said.
Jack was disappointed in Tommy's answer.
"And he never did anything to boast about—he was just a good man?"
"That's right," the professor said.
"He was just a good, honest man who loved his family and took care of everyone.
He lived the best life of all, better than any rich or famous man."
When the twins returned to school, Demi seemed more serious and tackled his math assignments with gusto.
This puzzled the professor because Demi had always hated math.
"I'm going to be a bookkeeper like my father," Demi explained one day.
Another day he said to Jo, "Papa told me to take care of my mother and the girls—what can I do to earn some money?"
"He didn't mean now," Jo said, ruffling her nephew's hair affectionately.
But Demi looked so disappointed that she quickly added, "I'm sure we could pay you to rake leaves."
As time passed, Jo gave him more jobs.
Demi was happy when he could provide a dollar each for his mother, Daisy, and baby Josy.
He often said the words "my father" with gentle pride and announced that he wanted to be called John when he was older.
On cold autumn nights, the children gathered around the fireplace in the schoolroom.
They read or played games while snacking on popcorn, nuts, and apples.
Their favorite activity was telling stories, but one October evening, they ran out of tales.
"Let's make a rule that the next person who enters the room must tell us a story," Nat said.
"It'll be amusing to see who comes in first!"
The others agreed with eager grins, and soon Jo arrived, looking for something.
The children waited until Jo took a few steps into the room and then pounced on her, demanding a story.
Jo laughed as Dan guided her over to the big chair.
"You sly cats—am I the first story mouse you've caught?" she asked.
"Yes!" they all said at once.
"Now, what should my story be about?"
"Boys!" the boys shouted.
"A brave girl!" Nan called out.
"Do you have any ideas, Daisy?" Jo asked kindly, trying to draw her into the conversation.
But Daisy, who'd been very quiet since her father died, just shrugged.
Jo looked back at the other children's excited faces and began her story.
"James Snow and his mother were poor and lived in a small house.
James was supposed to help his mother, but he preferred to read."
"Did James get in trouble for reading too much?" Nan asked.
"No, in fact, his mother let him read while she did everything around the house," Jo said.
"Oh, that's not right," said Demi, who was quite proud of helping his widowed mother.
Jo continued with her story.
"One autumn James wanted to attend school, but he didn't have money for schoolbooks.
The local minister agreed to help on one condition: James had to fill his mother's woodbox all winter."
"Chopping wood is so easy!" Dan said.
Jo smiled and went on, "At first it was easy to gather enough wood,
but in November, the weather grew cold, and James' mother burned lots of wood.
At one point she had to spend her own money for more."
"James was in trouble!" Nan said gleefully.
"Fortunately James realized he needed to work," Jo said, "so he did anything he could to earn money.
The minister was so proud of James that he secretly sent a new saw to the boy.
And James was so grateful that he kept his mother's woodbox full all winter. The end."
"Would it help my mother if I cut wood for her?" Demi asked.
"It might," Jo said as Rob walked into the room, dragging his quilt behind him.
"You're already helping her, Demi, and your father would be proud."
"Mama, I can't sleep!" Rob said, heading straight for Jo and climbing into her lap.
"You'd better go back to bed, Rob," Jack said.
"Everyone who comes in has to tell a story, and you can't do that."
"Yes, I can! I tell Teddy lots of stories about bears and moons and talking bugs!"
"Tell us one right now," Dan said, prepared to carry Rob back to bed.
"Let me think," Rob said.
"Getting up in the middle of the night runs in this family," Jo mused.
"I was always hopping in and out of bed as a child."
"Demi used to do it too!" Daisy exclaimed, her face bright with excitement.
Jo glanced at Daisy, delighted to hear her sounding happy. "Yes, he—"
"I've got a story now!" Rob interrupted.
"Once upon a time, a lady had a million children and one nice little boy.
She told him not to go outside, but he did and fell into the well with a loud splash."
After this startling beginning, Rob paused for breath.
"Is that all?" Jack asked.
"No, there's more." Rob wrinkled his brow in concentration for a few seconds.
"What did the lady do when the boy fell into the well?" Jo prompted her son.
"She used the bucket to get him out, and then she wrapped him in newspaper and put him on a shelf to dry, like a seed drying out."
Everyone laughed at this silly story, with Daisy adding, "That's how I dried my flower seeds."
"Exactly! And now it's time for bed," Jo said, scooping up Rob and making her escape.
"I wonder who'll come in next," said Daisy, who was beginning to enjoy herself.
When they heard footsteps in the hall, Nan ran to the door and cried, "Asia, come in!"
"No, no!" Asia laughed and was careful to stay in the hall.
"Mrs. Bauer warned me!"
So Asia managed to avoid the children, but they soon heard someone new humming.
"It's Mr. Bauer!" Tommy said, "and if we laugh loudly, he'll wonder what the joke is."
Sure enough, the professor couldn't resist the sound of laughter—especially since some of it was coming from Demi and Daisy.
"What's going on?" he said, walking right into the children's trap.
"You're telling us a story!" Dan explained their game and led him to the storyteller's chair.
The professor thought for a moment and then told a story about Grandpa March and a robber.
After Grandpa March was kind to him, the robber didn't have the heart to take any money.
"That was a short story—tell us another one!" Nat complained.
"No, too many stories are as bad as too many cookies," the professor said.
He jumped up and ran down the hall with everyone chasing him.
However, he had a good head start and safely reached his study.
"Good night, everyone!" he called through the closed door.
That year the children were especially proud of their contributions to Thanksgiving dinner.
"My herbs made the stuffing really delicious," Nan said with her mouth full.
Jack scooped another potato onto his plate and said, "These are the best potatoes I've ever eaten!"
"Has everyone had some of my beans?" Nat asked.
"Of course!" Tommy said. "You grew so many that Asia said we must all eat three helpings!"
"The pies came from my giant pumpkin," Rob said, "and wait till you see—"
"Hush!" Daisy said, giving her cousin a gentle swat. "It's a surprise!"
But the professor had overheard them and was curious.
"Daisy, I know you helped bake many pies, but Rob's pumpkin was enormous.
What did you do with the rest of it?"
"Well . . . uh . . . " Daisy hesitated.
Dan rescued Daisy by handing a bowl of nuts to Mr. Bauer. "Sir, try these!"
The professor looked down the table, murmuring to Jo, "Everyone seems to be in on this secret except me, but I can wait."
After dinner they all went for a long walk.
Then they waited impatiently for the rest of the family to arrive:
Mr. and Mrs. March, Aunt Meg and baby Josy, Uncle Laurie and Aunt Amy with Bess and a special guest.
"Mr. Hyde!" Dan exclaimed, immediately recognizing the naturalist. "What are you doing here?"
"I thought he'd like to see how well you're doing," Laurie said. "We're so proud of you."
"What a fine, polite young man you've turned into," Mr. Hyde said to Dan.
Dan and Mr. Hyde went to a parlor to talk until it was time for the evening's entertainment.
Then everyone went into the schoolroom, where Jack amazed the audience by solving math problems in his head.
Tommy won the spelling bee, and Dan performed gymnastics.
"Dan's a strong lad," Mr. Hyde said to the professor.
"When I go to South America in a few years, I'd like to take him along."
Overhearing that remark, Dan smiled, grateful to both Mr. Hyde and the Bauers.
"Where did the other children go?" the professor asked.
"Back here!" said a muffled voice behind a curtain made of blankets.
"Shh!" said more voices amid lots of giggles.
The curtain rose to reveal Bess as Cinderella.
Dressed in a ragged pinafore, she sat before a cardboard fireplace, not moving until Daisy whispered loudly, "Now!"
"Oh, I wish I could go to the ball!" Cinderella said.
Laurie clapped enthusiastically for his daughter, and Amy whispered, "My little darling!"
"You must not speak to me!" scolded Cinderella, looking at her parents.
The back of the fireplace opened like a door, and Nan appeared as the fairy godmother.
Dressed in a red cloak and pointed hat, she struggled to get through the opening.
"You [i@shall@i] go to the ball!" the fairy godmother said, tapping Cinderella with her wand.
"Now you must show my pretty dress," Cinderella said, tugging on her pinafore.
"No, no," Nan said in her own voice. "First you say, 'How can I go in these rags?'"
"Oh, that's right!" Cinderella said, and repeated Nan's words.
With that, the fairy godmother unfastened Cinderella's pinafore to reveal a beautiful pink dress.
She placed a crown on Cinderella's head and gave her silver paper slippers.
"But you have no coach!" the fairy godmother declared, waving her wand.
Cinderella was too busy admiring her slippers to say her next line, so Silas just leaped into action from backstage.
"Ready, Daisy?" he whispered. "Push!"
Suddenly four rats appeared, pulling a magnificent coach made from Rob's pumpkin and Teddy's wagon.
As the coachman, Teddy helped Cinderella into the coach and squeezed in beside her.
Cinderella waved to the audience, and that was the end of the first scene.
